en: *Eulogy on the Essential Meaning of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Volume One, composed by the Śramaṇa Tanguang of the Ximing Monastery in the Capital.
Now, the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is wordless; it must be distinguished through words. The true principle is devoid of marks; it requires...
Provisional marks are used to manifest the truth;
because words are identical with reality,
though there is speaking, there is no speaking.
Because the marks are identical with reality,
they manifest forms while remaining formless;
they speak without speaking.
What speech could fail to exhaust it?
It is the mark of the markless.
What form or appearance could fail to encompass it?
Therefore it is said that not [attaining] the name of "endowment" is itself the teaching of the Dharma;
there is no dharma that can be spoken— this is what is called the teaching of the Dharma.
This is the true essence of Prajñā,
the mother of all Awakened Ones.
It is for this reason that the four modes of birth remain obscured by accumulated delusions.
The followers of the Two Vehicles attain gradual enlightenment by severing the deeply hidden ignorance;
the Buddhas, however, realize it through direct experience.
They accomplish the four indestructible bodies.
The Bodhisattvas accord with and cultivate the three wisdoms that sever the two extremes,
thereby manifesting this wondrous function.
Transcending all other scriptures,
it metaphorically employs the diamond to manifest wondrous wisdom.
Since the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future abide in this very way,
so too do the great sages and the lesser sages.
Because one should cultivate it in this manner,
Subhūti elucidated the true pivot,
and the Tathāgata proclaimed the profound purport.
Through three questions and nine parables,
[the text] elucidates from beginning to end the eight attachments and five perversions.
When the mind and words are purified and perfected,
this is indeed the true entrustment and protection;
it is that which ensures the lineage of the Buddhas remains unbroken.
It serves as the pivotal hinge of the Vaipulya teachings and the essential bolt of the Great Sūtras;
its words are concise, yet their meaning is profound and far-reaching.
The phrasing is dense while the principles are all-encompassing;
those who seek to expound it cannot find its fundamental source,
and those who recite and uphold it [are likewise lost].
Since they merely cultivate its chapters and verses,
I, Maitreya, the one who succeeds me,
have composed this initial commentary on the stanzas to illuminate their profound mysteries.
It serves as the ultimate guide for proclamation and the standard for debaters; thus,
it was made for the first sage, Asaṅga.
Arranged in sequence, they abide in practice.
First, Bandhusena, a deity of the neighboring stage,
dispels the multitude of doubts at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The *Vajrasattva-ācārya-kathā* unifies the single reality within emptiness and existence;
the *Guṇaprabha-śāstra* gives rise to the two wisdoms within the ultimate and the conventional.
Each shall set forth their refined perspectives to collectively explicate this text;
though these may be called divergent schools, [they share a common purpose].
All [these teachings] ascend to the ultimate subtlety.
If one does not synthesize and harmonize these various doctrines,
how can one thoroughly extol the profound tenet?
I have compiled these divergent paths to follow the same principle, employing this to penetrate the underlying logic and open the profound gateway.

As for the title *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: it is so named because it cuts through all doubts with the diamond-like wisdom that transcends all phenomena. It is called "Prajñāpāramitā" (Perfection of Wisdom) because it is the ultimate realization of the nature of reality, wherein all dharmas are empty of self-nature and there is no dharma to be attained. It is called a "Sūtra" because it is the teaching expounded by the Buddha, which serves as the path for sentient beings to cross over from the shore of birth and death to the shore of nirvana. Thus, the title is established to reveal the essence of the scripture and to guide practitioners toward the goal of liberation.
This is precisely reaching the other shore.
It is the teaching of wisdom that can sever [delusion],
integrating principle and phenomena within the stages of practice.
Therefore, it is called wisdom;
because it shatters the stubborn accumulation of doubt and attachment,
it is metaphorically likened to the vajra.
Transcending birth and death to reach nirvana—
this is called "reaching the other shore.
Pervading both the phenomena and their underlying principles, it encompasses all classes of beings.
Taking this as the sūtra,
it is therefore called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
This [work] provides a commentary and explanation of this sūtra.
The analysis is presented in five sections:
first, an account of the causes for the emergence of the teaching;
second, an exposition of the essential purport of the sutra.
Third, revealing the majestic power of the sutra;
fourth, clarifying the intended audience of the sutra;
fifth, praising the main body of the sutra's text.
First, the origin of the teaching is described;
based on the sūtras and śāstras,
four general meanings are set forth.
First, to uproot suffering;
second, to bestow happiness;
third, to cause the arousal of practice.
Fourth, causing them to attain the fruit.
Regarding the phrase "uprooting suffering":
it means to eliminate for sentient beings the suffering of old age, illness, death, impermanence, and the like.
The Sūtra says: "By means of these three matters,
the Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world for the sake of all sentient beings."
Regarding the statement "the teaching of the realization of the Dharma" and so forth:
although this is stated in general terms,
it also applies specifically.
The Dharma realized by the Buddha is solely true prajñā; therefore,
it is taught by setting aside three matters.
This sutra causes those of the four modes of birth and so forth to all enter the state of nirvana without remainder;
it merely extinguishes their birth,
for there is no aging and so forth.
It does not arise abiding in form and so forth;
its mental states and thoughts do not arise,
because it is free from the causes of arising.
Regarding the phrase "bestowing bliss," it refers to the bliss of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for sentient beings;
this knowledge and vision is itself bodhi and nirvana.
This sutra was taught in order to reveal that which is capable of being known and seen, both in terms of the fruit and the cause.
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says:
"The Buddhas appear in the world for one sole great purpose."
The opening, revealing, awakening, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,
as well as all Buddhas and the Dharma,
are born from this sutra.
The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas.
To see that this mark is no-mark is to see the Tathāgata.
To be free from all marks is precisely what is called the Buddhas;
this is, in sequence, the teaching, the revealing, the awakening, and the entry.
The scriptural passages are not uniform;
one should seek them out and cite them.
As for the statement regarding "arising and practicing":
Because externalists and others initiate their practice according to the dharmas appropriate to them; therefore,
[it is stated] in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-śāstra*.
It is said that the six causes are taught for the purpose of severing doubt and for the purpose of giving rise to faith and understanding.
For the sake of entering into the profound meaning;
for the sake of non-retrogression;
and for the sake of generating joy.
It is for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma;
that is to say, it causes the lineage of the Buddhas to be uninterrupted through the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
How is it that this lineage remains uninterrupted?
It severs the doubts of those of the two vehicles and others regarding their own lack of share [in the Dharma],
causing them to enter the Great Dharma;
therefore, it is called "Severing Doubts."
At the initial stage of grasping signs,
the mind is not yet settled;
it is for the purpose of generating settled conviction.
This is called "arousing resolute belief.
As for what is meant by "certain belief," it is because it causes one to enter the unconditioned principle of the two kinds of emptiness.
This is called "entering the profound," meaning that having attained the stages of mastery,
one then delights in dwelling in tranquility.
Because it causes one to advance in practice,
it is called "non-retrogression.
Once one has already advanced in practice, [it is called]...
To attain that which cannot be attained,
and to rejoice in this of one's own accord,
is called the arising of joy.
Upon hearing the Dharma, one experiences joy and consolation;
by then explaining it to others and causing it to circulate everywhere,
it is called "the long endurance of the Dharma."
Because of this dharma, benefit extends universally to both oneself and others; therefore,
it is said that the lineage of the Buddhas through Prajñā is never severed.
Following the cited passages,
the meaning of the extensive treatise is explained.
Regarding the phrase "attaining the fruit":
Because one attains the fruit of non-abiding by relying upon the two truths,
the Bodhisattva Guṇaprabha states in his treatise: "Regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha..."
All are subsumed within the two truths.
The first is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
which refers to the provisional and differentiated characteristics of persons and phenomena.
The second is ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
which is the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) of both persons and phenomena.
These are the ultimate and the conventional.
Their substance is not separate,
for the conventional is itself the ultimate;
thus they exist, yet do not exist.
Because the ultimate is identical to the conventional,
it is empty yet not empty;
it is neither existent nor empty.
The principle herein is that,
by attaining the Middle Way,
one does not abide in either of the two extremes.
Because of this non-abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa,
one achieves the Great Parinirvāṇa of No-Abode; therefore,
the Buddha preached this sūtra.
This causes one to awaken to the two truths; that is,
by observing the conventional as the ultimate,
one becomes detached from all marks.
Right knowledge arises; that is,
one truly contemplates the conventional,
for there is nothing it does not penetrate.
There arises subsequent knowledge;
because compassion is aroused by means of this subsequent knowledge,
[beings] are born within the four modes of birth and the three realms.
He causes all to enter parinirvāṇa;
yet because he abides nowhere by virtue of true wisdom,
in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.
Because they have generated wisdom and do not abide [in it];
because they do not abide in saṃsāra, yet give rise to compassion to deliver sentient beings;
and thus they do not abide in nirvāṇa.
This immediately constitutes the fruit of the great nirvana of non-abiding.
The same applies to all subsequent passages;
one should seek them out and cite them accordingly.
The exposition of the origin having been concluded,
that which clarifies the intended meaning is further divided into two parts.
First, the tenet system is revealed;
second, the goal to be reached is clarified.
There are three tenets.
These are the three types of *prajñā*.
Although it is taught elsewhere that there are five kinds,
here we follow the *Jñānaprasthāna* and its analogies.
The first is the true aspect (*dharmatā*),
which is the wondrous principle of suchness (*tathatā*) free from marks.
The second is contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*).
Third is the syllable, which refers to the words, phrases, and phonemes that serve as the means for conveying the signless, wondrous wisdom arising from reality.
The first is the nature;
the second is the characteristic;
the last is the cause.
Since both wisdom and its basis are called *prajñā*,
when the objects and attendants are added, they constitute five.
Since this is not the central tenet of the sūtra—
as explained elsewhere—
although there are three types [of suffering], [it is not the primary meaning].
That which we now take as our primary authority consists precisely of the former two,
while also being fully conversant with the written word.
Without the wisdom that contemplates the true nature of reality, it does not arise;
without the principle of contemplating the true nature of reality, it is not revealed.
Therefore, the object and the wisdom are the primary basis of our doctrine.
As for these written words,
they are merely provisional tools;
once realization is attained, the teachings themselves are transcended.
Since it is not explicitly stated as the primary clarification,
yet serves as a supporting reason (*hetu*),
it is also included among the tenets (*siddhānta*).
There are four points of orientation.
First is the teaching of Prajñā,
which refers to the discourse on non-discourse regarding the means [of expression], such as names and so forth.
This is the true skillful means (*upāya*), because it accords with reality.
Second is the prajñā of principle (*li*),
which refers to the wondrous principle attained through "attainment as non-attainment."
Because it is able to verify the non-erroneous characteristics through the fishing net [of skillful means],
there is the threefold practice of prajñā;
that is, practicing the six perfections in a manner that is without practice and without signs.
Because it is the cause capable of inducing and realizing the unsurpassed [state],
it is the fourth fruit: prajñā.
There is nothing to be attained,
yet there is attainment; for Bodhi and Nirvana are that which serves as the means of realization for the unsurpassed fruit.
These four types of the Prajñā teachings toward which one proceeds are shallow in expression but profound in principle;
they distinguish the stages of practice and the fulfillment of the fruit.
This is what has been explained.
It is precisely the fruit of principle;
it is that which is to be reached through the medium of words,
for it is the profound and perfect Dharma.
Furthermore, although the teachings and practices are said to be of a superficial level,
they are nonetheless the provisional means by which one returns to the ultimate; thus concludes the clarification of the fundamental tenets.
Regarding "power and majesty," this briefly indicates that this sutra possesses ten powers and majesties,
which are like a vajra.
Therefore, it receives this name:
first, the most supreme power;
the most excellent and foremost, most rare dharma.
Because wherever it is located, it should be revered;
it is like that vajra which surpasses all precious objects.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Just as among all jewels, the diamond is the most supreme,
for it conforms to the matrix of those jewels and becomes that very jewel.
Second is the power that is difficult to perceive;
both the meaning of the sutras and their karmic fruits are inconceivable.
Because those who delight in inferior teachings are unable to receive it;
just as that vajra cannot be seen by anyone other than [the one capable of seeing it].
Therefore, the Nyāya says:
"The crest-jewel of Śakra is named Vajra."
Others are unable to see it because its brilliant radiance overwhelms them.
Third is the power of averting calamities.
Those who uphold this sutra with inferior resolve will be treated with contempt by others due to the karmic offenses of their past lives.
Because it is further extinguished;
just as that vajra can eliminate calamities and poisons,
according to the *Satyavādin-vyākaraṇa*.
There are six kinds of jewels, all of which are named vajra;
they are of two colors: blue and green.

It universally benefits all sentient beings,
is able to adorn and purify the buddha-lands,
and brings about the attainment of bodhi.
Just as that vajra fulfills the wishes of people,
so too are the other four colors among the six jewels:
yellow, red, white, and sky-blue.
Fifth is the power of solidity, by which one can travel through space at will and emerge from water or fire.
It can destroy the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span;
for it is not destroyed by the marks of phenomena or non-phenomena.
Just as that vajra cannot be destroyed by those things.
Therefore, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
"Wherever the vajra is aimed,
there is nothing it cannot shatter."
Furthermore, because this vajra is indestructible,
it possesses the sixth utility of power:
penetrating the realization of non-self.
One attains the stage of patience because one fully knows and perceives through the Buddha-eye and other such faculties.
Just as that vajra pierces through all things,
the Liang-era *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) says:
For example, just as a diamond is sharp by nature and is therefore able to pierce and cut through all things,
so too is the power of the seven immediate [retributions].
One practices giving without dwelling upon it,
giving rise to a mind that is non-abiding;
thus, characteristics are themselves non-characteristics.
Because there is nothing to be apprehended.
Just as that vajra is not a material object and is unmixed,
so it is said in the Abhidharma:
For example, the substance of a diamond is without interstices because it cannot be interspersed with sand, stones, or the like;
this is the eighth power of uniform flavor.
All are distinguished by means of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena is that they are all the Buddha-dharma.
Just as that vajra is of a single, uniform substance,
the Abhidharma states:
"For example, a vajra is of a single nature."
It is pure and unadulterated because it is immutable.
Ninth, it can induce majestic power.
All Buddhas and the Dharma are born from this,
for it accomplishes inconceivable and boundless merit.
Just as that vajra can attract all manner of treasures,
the Liang Dynasty *She dasheng lun* states:
"The vajra can summon all precious objects."
Because jewels spontaneously gather where there is a vajra-place,
its pervasive power fills the ten directions,
and its merit is as vast as space.
It benefits all,
is free from all marks, and delivers all.
Just as that vajra pervades all things,
the Abhidharma states:
"For example, it is like a vajra-wheel and so forth, which pervade all locations."
Because it pervades the entire world,
there are further textual passages;
these should be cited and explained as appropriate.
The manifestation of majestic power is concluded.
Regarding the suitability of the faculties for those who are to be converted,
there are two parts within this section.
First, the nature of the faculties is distinguished;
subsequently, the application of the teaching is clarified.
Within the distinction of the nature of the faculties:
It is further divided into two:
first, the ultimate remoteness of the direct cause;
second, the proximate differentiation of the contributory causes.
That which is called the ultimate remoteness of the true cause refers to the tree-penetrating *tathatā* of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). From the very beginning,
there is in reality no dual nature between ordinary beings and sages.
Sentient beings and Buddhas share a single, equal cause; therefore,
in reality, there is no distinction of spiritual lineage (gotra).
It is solely due to the varying degrees of thickness and thinness of ignorance that there are differences between the false and the correct regarding the teachings one hears.
Because the causes and conditions of the Buddha-dharma involve the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as the sudden and gradual approaches,
it is said that sentient beings possess various kinds of realms (*dhātu*).
Due to the power of the熏習 (vāsanā) of internal and external causes and conditions upon its single essence,
the causal Buddha-nature.
Because all ultimately attain unsurpassed bodhi,
it is said that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature.
As for what is called the "conditional cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*), which is proximate and distinct from the nature itself:
This refers to the horizontal suppression and immediate perfuming of the five natures;
first, the nature of lacking the seed-potential (agotra),
which refers to those classes for whom ignorance is dense and heavy.
Due to the power of causes and conditions such as being defiled by heterodox teachings and the like,
they slander the True Dharma.
Denying cause and effect,
they incinerate all seeds of the roots of goodness; therefore,
it cannot yet be predicted when they will emerge from the world.
That is to say, the *icchantika* is called one who lacks the spiritual lineage (*agotra*).
Second is the nature of the *śrāvaka*,
which refers to one who has previously heard the teaching on the Four Noble Truths.
By the power of joyful delight,
the seeds of consciousness are perfumed;
by the power of these seeds, [the result arises].
They feel profound revulsion toward birth and death,
seeking only their own liberation,
and do not aspire to benefit others.
By means of this, one shall attain the minor fruit of a śrāvaka;
this very seed is termed the "śrāvaka-nature."
Third is the nature of a pratyekabuddha,
which refers to one who, having previously heard the teaching on the twelve links of dependent origination,
has developed a joyful inclination toward it through the power of that aspiration.
It is perfumed to form seeds;
by the power of these seeds,
one delights in one's own tranquility.
Contemplating the principle of dependent origination and relinquishing the mind of both teaching and listening,

its actual merit does not equal the blessing of upholding even a single four-line verse of this sutra;
for the former involves the physical and mental suffering of currently abandoning the body.

How much more so when one seeks the fruit of a dharma that leads to future suffering and practices giving, where both cause and effect are suffering—how can this be compared to the superior merit of upholding this sutra?
For this sutra possesses seven kinds of superior capabilities; when one upholds and explains it, both cause and effect are blissful.
Therefore, it surpasses the merit of giving up the body.
Thus, Vasubandhu’s commentary expresses this meaning in verse:
"The suffering of the body is superior to that; It is marvelous and possesses the highest significance."
That wisdom is a shore difficult to measure, And unlike other dharmas, it is firm and solid;
it understands the profound meaning, Surpassing other sūtras,
it is the great cause and is pure— The most excellent merit among all merits.
The first line explains the wording of this sutra passage to demonstrate that the merit of this sutra is superior.
The subsequent six lines explain the following sutra passage,
citing seven kinds of causes to explain the reason for its superiority.
The final phrase summarizes the excellence of the merit.
The Sūtra says:
"At that time... up to this sūtra. The Commentary says:
This is the compassionate response of Subhūti.
Hearing that giving away many bodies is not equal to the merit of this sūtra,
he realizes and understands this sūtra as the cause for bodhi.
At the height of the joy of the Dharma regarding this profound and wondrous principle, he was moved to compassion.

He thought: "In the past, when I attained the true wisdom of the Path and realized the unconditioned, although I possessed what is called the 'eye of wisdom,' I had never heard of such a rare teaching."
This dharma-gate within the meaning is truly rare.
According to other versions of the sutra, there is further text below this which reads: "For what reason? The Buddha says that the *prajñāpāramitā* is not [in fact] the *prajñāpāramitā*."
This refers to the dharma-gate among the seven meanings;
it explains the passage in the first verse concerning the boundless wisdom of the supreme meaning.
The phrase "For what reason?
interrogates the cause for not hearing.
The passage beginning with "The Buddha having spoken" explains the cause for not hearing.
Because this shore of wisdom has two meanings,
although one possesses the eye of insight, one has not yet heard it.
The first is because it signifies the supreme excellence of the shore of wisdom.
Therefore it is said, "The Buddha preached the Prajñāpāramitā.
Second, because the shore of wisdom is difficult to measure,
it is said, "It is not [a fixed] Prajñāpāramitā."
Because these two meanings distinguish it particularly from other sūtras,
it is collectively described as the foremost among the Dharma-gates. Sūtra.
The World-Honored One possesses most rare and marvelous merits. The commentary states:
Next, the attachment to the notion that the merit of hearing has already arisen in accordance with its meaning is refuted.
Within this, there are two parts.
The first part provides a general indication of its superior capacity;
the latter part dispels misconceptions regarding it.
This is the former.
In order to shatter their indolence regarding gain and honor and to incite them to apply themselves with diligence,
it is said that upholding this sutra is superior to the merit of sacrificing one's body.
One should not, however, grasp at this literally as if it were a literal comparison of actual merits.
If one can give rise to the wisdom of the true mark by relying on this sutra of the true mark and exert diligent effort,
you should know that such a person is the most rare and extraordinary of all.
— Sūtra.
"The World-Honored One arrives at what is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states: This sweeps away emotional conceptions. To speak of the "true mark" means that non-marking is itself the mark;
it is for the purpose of causing one to depart from false attachments.
This does not mean that this true mark exists as such.
Rather, when one departs from falsehood and accords with the signless,
the Buddha therefore calls it the "true mark."
Since this sutra elucidates the principle of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) where other sutras have not yet done so,
it differs from those other sutras.
Thus, among the seven meanings set forth in the verse, this is also unlike other dharmas.
The Sūtra says:
"World-Honored One, it is not difficult [to understand]. The Commentary states:
Next, the minor bodhisattvas are led to give rise to a sense of shame and remorse and to exert themselves.
This section contains two parts;
first, that it is not difficult to encounter the Buddha’s teaching and accept it with faith.
In the future, it will be truly rare for anyone to believe and uphold this;
this is the first [instance].
It is for the sake of inspiring shame and remorse in a certain class of bodhisattvas who harbor indolence, thereby urging them toward diligence.
Therefore, it is said that even in an evil age there are still those who uphold and proclaim [the Dharma];
how much more so when the Buddha is present in a favorable age—why would one not exert diligent effort?
This is intended to stir them to a sense of shame and remorse, giving rise to a mind of earnest endeavor.
The Sūtra says: "To say, 'I now believe, understand, accept, and uphold [this]' is not difficult.
But as for the future age reaching that which is most rare... The commentary says:
That one will believe and uphold it in the future is truly rare.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation.
This is the first [point].
In an age of many obstacles and difficulties, where the world and its beings are inferior and the capacity for understanding subtle [truths] is slight,
if one merely gives rise to faith, [one attains this].
If there are those who deeply understand the meanings and principles, retaining the text in their mouths while grasping the significance in their hearts,
you should know that such persons are the most rare and extraordinary.
— Sūtra.
"Why is this so? up to "the mark of a life-span. The commentary states:
The following explains the reason.
The text is further divided into three parts.
First, one attains realization of the emptiness of the self;
next, one awakens to the emptiness of phenomena;
finally, one accords with all Buddhas.
However, all three passages contain evidence and explanations;
these demonstrate the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
For what reason, then, should one believe, understand, accept, and uphold them?
Such a person is the most rare and extraordinary,
for they are able to sever and subdue the notions of a personal self and a self in others. Sūtra.
Why is this so? Because it arrives at that which is precisely the absence of marks (*animitta*). [The commentary] says:
This is the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Regarding "the absence of self," etc.:
Why is this so? Because one realizes the emptiness of phenomena by relying on the sūtras;
since the grasping at a self arises from the grasping at phenomena, if one eliminates the grasping at phenomena, the view of a self is naturally removed.
"How could there be any marks? Because these marks are non-marks, they are the emptiness of phenomena.
[The Sūtra says:
"For what reason... this is called the Buddhas. The Commentary states:
This means they accord with all Buddhas.
Why are they able to be free from the views of self and dharmas?
Because those who uphold this sutra accord with all Buddhas.
The Buddha is free from delusive appearances;
his wisdom is firm and solid, capable of acceding to that which is profound and subtle,
and he has therefore preached this sutra.
Those who receive and uphold the profound and subtle meaning expounded by the sūtras act in accordance with the Buddha and give rise to firm and wondrous wisdom;
for they are able to eliminate the two types of grasping.
In future ages, those who believe, understand, accept, and uphold [this teaching] will be most rare and extraordinary;
this refers to the "firm and solid" and "profoundly subtle" aspects among the seven meanings summarized in verse.
Sūtra:
The Buddha told [them], "This is exceedingly rare. The commentary states:
Next, he refutes the fear and lack of diligence found among those of the Two Vehicles.
In the past, when the Tathāgata was within the teachings for the Two Vehicles...
It is taught that all phenomena exist, namely the aggregates, bases, and so forth;
it is also taught that phenomena are empty, namely selflessness and so forth.
Both the conditioned and the unconditioned are all said to exist.
Now, this sutra is explained through the refutation by means of emptiness.
At the time of hearing it, if one hears that "dharmas exist" and then [immediately] says they are non-existent,
there is a fear that this sutra might be considered not the correct path.
Just as one experiences fear and trepidation when walking in improper places such as pits and ravines,
so too, upon hearing the Dharma of emptiness,
the mind becomes hesitant and unable to sever doubt; thus, it gives rise to terror.
After reflecting thus, their alarm and dread deepen further;
they turn back resolutely and give rise to a total sense of awe and trepidation.
Now, this sutra also reaches those of the two vehicles, causing them to turn their minds toward supreme enlightenment.
Since one is unable to exert diligence due to such states as fear,
this [text] now refutes them so as to inspire diligence;
that is to say, the principle of reality is free from the two extremes.
If one clings to the existence of emptiness, it does not accord with the Middle Way.
To destroy such clinging to characteristics, the two absences are taught;
this is not to say that phenomena such as existence and emptiness are entirely non-existent.
It is rare that those of the two vehicles and others can awaken to this principle without being struck with fear or alarm.

Furthermore, this sutra reveals the three natures of non-essence (*trisvabhāva*) in order to dismantle the mind's attachments to the emptiness or existence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
This does not mean that they deny the existence of the two [natures], the dependent and the perfected; rather,
it means that when the followers of the Two Vehicles and others hear of the "naturelessness of characteristics," they do not become startled,
and when they hear of the "naturelessness of arising," they do not become terrified.
Because they do not fear the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature,
all are truly marvelous. Thus says the Sūtra.
"Why is it that one reaches the perfections? The commentary states:
Next arises non-negligence, which is the second locus of shame and remorse.
Within the text, there is an inquiry and explanation as to what the reason is for not being terrified and so forth.
One should say that such a person is indeed rare;
for it is because this sutra possesses three superior excellences that it causes those who hear it not to be startled or terrified, which is itself a rarity.
First, because it excels other sūtras;
that is to say, among the meanings expounded by the six perfections,
it uniquely expounds the perfection of wisdom as the guide and so forth.
That is to say, among the seven meanings, this [sūtra] excels other sūtras for two reasons:
first, it can serve as a great cause;
"great" refers to the fruition of Buddhahood, namely bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Because the non-conceptual wisdom expressed by this [term] is able to give birth to the Dharma-body and Reward-body Buddhas,
it constitutes the meaning of the "Great Cause" within the seven meanings.
Based on these two meanings,
the Sūtra states that the Tathāgata speaks of the "first pāramitā" and so forth;
for both the signifier and the signified are preeminent.
The statement "it is not" destroys the mind that grasps at signs.
Third, because it is taught by all Buddhas alike;
as the other original text states: "Those immeasurable Buddhas also speak of this foremost pāramitā."
This refers precisely to the meaning of purity among the seven meanings.
Because the Buddhas have equally realized this principle of purity,
they likewise speak of it in the same way that they have realized it.
This sutra contains such supreme and exalted teachings of the two vehicles;
yet now you are able to believe and uphold it without being startled or terrified.
You bodhisattvas—how can you be negligent and fail to practice with diligence?

Having already exhorted those bodhisattvas who are attached to gain and profit and are indolent to give rise to shame and remorse in the previous second passage, this current section further causes those bodhisattvas who fail to initiate diligence and are negligent to give rise to shame and remorse; this is called the second point.
Since it has been taught that this sutra possesses seven kinds of superior causes that surpass the merit of giving away one's body,
a bodhisattva should therefore abandon indolence and gain,
and instead constantly and diligently cultivate this sutra of superior causes.
Sūtra:
Subhūti [speaks] up to the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Commentary:
Next follows the ninth [section], which abandons the obstacle of the suffering of intolerance.
This is the thirteenth dwelling place, Enduring Suffering.
One severs the eighth link, the fruition of suffering that has already come into being, and so forth, thereby severing the three kinds of doubt.
Relying upon the sūtras, one practices the conduct of patience.
At the former place of offering,
cause them to practice making offerings according to this sutra so as to cultivate the provisions of merit;
and at the place free from indolence.
To cause them to arouse diligence,
he exhorts and encourages them by citing the superior benefits described in the sutras.
Even if one has achieved [realization], one must be able to endure suffering.
If one cannot endure suffering during the time of practice,
there will be regression, which constitutes an obstacle.
Patience is of three kinds and can eliminate the three types of suffering.
The first is the patience of discerning phenomena (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*).
Because they examine the principle of the two kinds of emptiness with precision,
they do not perceive the characteristics of suffering in the cycle of birth and death,
and are thus able to give rise to the great mind seeking the unsurpassed fruit.
Second is the patience of enduring suffering,
because one is able to endure cold, heat, and so forth,
and does not perceive the sufferings of fatigue, old age, illness, and the like.
One is able to arouse diligent effort to achieve the supreme fruit.
Third is patience toward enmity and harm,
because one is able to endure the enmity and harm inflicted by others.
Without abandoning compassion, one remains free from the signs of suffering and affliction;
thus, one is able to extensively gather and transform others to swiftly achieve the great fruit.
It is precisely through the initial patience that one can give rise to the latter two.
Because one observes the principle of emptiness, there is no enmity and so forth.
If the mind gives rise to views such as the notion of a self or phenomena, one perceives suffering;
if these do not arise, one would instead delight in saṃsāra.
Some delight in dwelling in tranquility and do not give rise to the great resolve;
unable to endure weariness and exhaustion, they fail to arouse diligence;
and upon seeing the suffering of enmity and harm, they give rise to a mind of retreat.
Consequently, this becomes an obstacle to the fruit of Buddhahood;
for these bodhisattvas are unable to rely on the sūtras to give rise to the three types of patience by abandoning the notions of self and person.
One might further doubt that this sutra can bring about bitter fruits [of karma],
arguing that because it involves abandoning the body— which is painful for both body and mind—
both cause and effect would be suffering.
Those of inferior merit experience suffering of both body and mind when practicing walking meditation and encountering cold, heat, and so forth.
How then can those of superior merit do so?
Because of their attachment, they are unable to give rise to patience based on the sūtras.
Because of doubt, one does not delight in the sutras that teach the arousal of patience (*kṣānti*).
Now, wishing to sever that mind of doubtful clinging and cause one to rely on the sutras to accomplish the practice of patience, it is said:
"There is no self, no person, and so forth, even when being cut to pieces."
Asaṅga defines it in terms of removing the obstacle of attachment, calling it "being free from the obstacle of intolerance";
Vasubandhu, however, approaches it from the perspective of severing the initial doubt, calling it "severing the fruit of suffering established by the sūtra.
Based on Asaṅga’s definition of being free from intolerance, the text is divided into four sections.
First, that which is capable of endurance is the essence of patience (*kṣānti*).
Second, it clarifies the characteristics of patience and the occasions for generating patience.
Third, the distinctions of patience are its various types.
The fourth clarification addresses the causes and conditions for the inability to endure;
this is the first [section].
Within the text, there are two sentences.
The first phrase means that one practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) in accordance with the true object as it has been realized;
that is, one gives rise to the three types of patience previously described in relation to the principle of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) as it has been realized.
Because they all arise based upon the true object,
the essence of patience (*kṣānti*) consists of non-aversion (*adveṣa*), diligence (*vīrya*), and wisdom (*prajñā*);
this is because it is like the state of non-aversion and so forth within the realized object.
Therefore, as previously stated:
"The patience that one is able to exercise, by relying on the true object and practicing true patience,
is the essence of the pure roots of goodness of the pāramitās."
Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of the "pāramitā of patience.
The subsequent phrase causes one to depart from the characteristic of patience regarding the true realm as it has been realized.
It is because of this departure from characteristics [that it is called a pāramitā].
This is the other shore, whose virtue is immeasurable;
it is the most supreme meaning,
capable of relinquishing the mark of self, the mark of anger, and the mark of suffering and affliction.
Not only is there no suffering, but there is also compassion and the harmonious union of shared joy.
For these reasons, the Sūtra states that it is "not patience" and so forth;
thus, one practices the patience that is free from signs, just as it has been realized.
Therefore, the treatise says: "As much as one is able to endure.
Since there is this patience that is free from signs, ascetic practices based on the sūtras are virtuous.
The verse of Vasubandhu’s commentary on this meaning says:
One who is able to endure ascetic practices, Because those ascetic practices possess goodness, their merit is immeasurable; Such is the most supreme meaning.
Free from the notions of self and ill-will, truly without suffering or affliction,
he dwells in shared joy and possesses compassion; such is the fruit of his ascetic practice,
and like that which was mentioned before, his merit is immeasurable.
This is because all [of these] are the fruits of suffering obtained through ascetic practices based on the sutras within this context. Therefore,
although one practices patience, there is the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā),
which differs from the case where abandoning the body results in the fruit of suffering.
[Sūtra]: Why is this?
[Commentary]: The following clarifies the characteristics of patience (*kṣānti*) and the locus for generating patience toward sentient beings (*sattvakṣānti*).
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the inquiry, and second, the explanation.
This is the former.
Based on what does the characteristic of patience arise?
Once patience has been produced, why then do you say it is not so? For what reason?
[Sūtra]:
"Subhūti, up to the point of having his body cut to pieces. [Commentary]:
Regarding the explanation below, there are two parts.
The first part clarifies the basis for the patience of non-arising;
the latter part correctly clarifies the characteristics of patience.
This is the former.
However, there are three types of patience that arise:
namely, patience toward enmity and harm arising from others;
and patience toward the acceptance of suffering arising from cold, heat, and so forth.
Regarding phenomena, we give rise to the patience of analytical investigation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-kṣānti*).
Herein, the bases for the arising of the three types of patience should be clarified;
within the characteristics of "inferior patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), the three types of patience should be elucidated.
As for the statement that "only those who endure resentment" are able to give rise to both the subject and object [of patience],
this is because the text is abbreviated; it cites the beginning to reveal the end,
thereby showing that in former times he acted as the Sage of Patience (Kṣāntivādin).
Because he was able to endure the suffering of having his body cut and mangled by King Kalabha without giving rise to a mind of anger,
the very place where others cause resentment and harm is precisely the locus where patience in enduring resentment arises.
Sūtra:
"At that time, I fell into the mark of a person (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*). Commentary:
The following clarifies the characteristics of patience (*kṣānti*).
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a direct explanation, and second, a reductio ad absurdum.
This is the former.
Because at that time there is no self and so forth,
the physical form is already free from other characteristics,
and thus there is no failure to perceive suffering and affliction.
Because it is possible to feel anger, one is able to give rise to the patience that endures enmity and harm.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
"If one encounters harm from others, one should reflect as follows:"
"This was my own past karma that deserved the harm from another;
if I do not now endure it, I will only increase the causes of suffering.
Since I am already bound by suffering," [he thought].
"How could this constitute self-love?
Having reflected thus, one should cultivate five perceptions.
The first is the perception of grasping.
Second, the perception of loving-kindness;
third, the perception of phenomena alone;
fourth, the perception of suffering.
Fifth is the perception of impermanence.
This does not give rise to the notion of a self regarding harm from others;
it is, among the five characteristics, solely the characteristic of dharmas.

Because one cultivates the realization that there is no self and only the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one does not retaliate against those who harm them; thus, the first patience (*kṣānti*) arises.
[Sūtra]:
For what reason? [Commentary]: It is said in praise:
The subsequent section, which returns to clarify the meaning of the Chinese text, is further divided into two parts:
first, the inquiry, and second, the explanation.
This is the former.
For what reason is it known that,
at that time, there were no marks such as "self" and so forth? Sūtra:
"In the past, I was one toward whom anger ought to have arisen. The commentary says:
This is an explanation.
Anger arises from the self.
If there were the view of a self, resentment would arise;
resentment is established based on anger.
Its nature consists of harboring malice without relinquishing it and forming a bond of enmity.
Since hatred lacks the characteristics of ignorance and a self,
when practicing patience, there are no such characteristics as "self" and so forth. Sūtra:
"Subhūti, up to the mark of a person. The commentary says:
The following clarifies the distinctions of patience;
that is, the patience of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*).
Regarding "patience by way of category":
this refers to the endurance of suffering that continues throughout five hundred successive lifetimes;
it is of the same category as the previously mentioned endurance of the extreme suffering of being cut and mangled.
Alternatively, because one constantly practices [patience] throughout five hundred lifetimes with similar conduct from beginning to end, it is called "patience of the same kind" (*jātisaha-kṣānti*).
Because it is not merely singular, it is termed "differentiated.
The "Patience Sage" (*kṣānti-ṛṣi*) is none other than the "Compassion Sage" (*maitrī-karuṇā-ṛṣi*).
[Sūtra]:
Therefore, [it leads] up to the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*. [Commentary]:
The following section clarifies the causes and conditions for the lack of forbearance (*akṣānti*) and their respective remedies.
The cause of non-endurance is the perception of the three types of suffering;
because one possesses the perception of suffering, one is unable to endure it.
Regarding the perception of the three types of suffering:
first is the perception of the suffering of abiding in saṃsāra;
second is the perception of the suffering of opposition among sentient beings.
Third is the perception of the suffering of lacking resources while dwelling [in cyclic existence].
Due to the first perception, one perceives the suffering of saṃsāra;
unable to endure birth and death, one does not give rise to the Great Resolve (mahācitta).
Consequently, one is unable to give rise to the patient acceptance that arises from discerning the Dharma (*dharmānupaśyanā-kṣānti*).
Because of the subsequent characteristic, one sees the suffering of hostility and harm and is unable to endure it;
thus, when sentient beings act in opposition, one is unable to give rise to the patient acceptance that endures hostility and harm (*āghātamarṣaṇa-kṣānti*).
Due to subsequent perceptions, one sees that there is a lack of necessities;
being unable to endure cold, heat, and so forth,
one is consequently unable to give rise to the patience of accepting suffering with equanimity.
Now, in order to counteract these three perceptions,
three types of superior patience— such as thorough investigation and so forth— are generated as antidotes; thus,
they are divided into three.
In the initial treatment of the causes and conditions of the suffering of saṃsāra,
the text is further divided into four sections:
the general heading, the individual explanations, the re-establishment through proof, and the concluding exhortation.
This is the first.
Now, regarding the patience toward the three types of suffering, there are both general and specific aspects.
General suffering refers to the initial perception of the suffering of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Because they do not correctly investigate the principle of the two kinds of emptiness,
they perceive the suffering of saṃsāra, perceive it as contradictory and harmful, and perceive their resources as insufficient;
consequently, they are unable to generate the bodhicitta.
Because one constantly dwells within birth and death, enduring the suffering of saṃsāra.
That treatise states:
"Those who have not yet generated the supreme bodhicitta possess such faults," and so forth.
General patience refers to the initial patience of discerning the Dharma;
because it is able to discern the principle of the two kinds of emptiness,
one perceives neither birth-and-death, nor weariness, nor harm from others.
By means of this, one is able to give rise to the bodhicitta and together realize bodhi,
for we emerge from saṃsāra as one.
As that treatise says:
By means of the mark of non-self, one is able to resolve the mind and cultivate the practice of patience and so forth.
As for the patience regarding specific sufferings,
this refers to the other two perceptions and two types of patience, each arising in dependence upon its respective object.
Because each [of these] is free from characteristics,
and because one now wishes to cause the abandonment of the general perception of suffering,
general patience (*sāmānyakṣānti*) is established as the antidote.
Therefore, it is said that one should generate the bodhicitta by remaining detached from all signs (*nimitta*). This is because,
through the thorough investigation of the principle of selflessness (*anātman*),
one is able to abandon the three types of perceptions of suffering associated with the notion of self (*ātman*).
Because one resolves to practice the perfection of patience,
Vasubandhu’s commentary states in verse:
"To give rise to the resolve not to abandon [sentient beings], One practices and remains steadfast."
"For the sake of the perfection of patience" (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
The first two lines pose the question and the latter two lines provide the answer.
"For the sake of" (*yad-artham*) means "in dependence upon."
On what basis does the mind not abandon the thought of enlightenment?
On what basis does one give rise to the aspects of practice and cultivate them?
And on what basis, through the perfection of patience regarding non-self and so forth, is it possible to generate the resolve for awakening?
Furthermore, by means of non-self, one is able to practice and attain firmness in that practice.
This explains the meaning of generating the bodhicitta that is free from all signs, as stated in the Sūtra. Sūtra:
"One should not abide in the mind arising from form up to contact with mental phenomena.
Commentary: This is a specific explanation.
If one clings to form and so forth as being substantially existent...
Consequently, they give rise to longing, nostalgia, and stinginess, which further increase their cyclic existence and cause them to dwell forever in birth and death.
How could they possibly abandon all signs and resolve for bodhicitta?
It is for the sake of preventing these things that [the teaching is given].
The Sūtra exhorts one not to give rise to a mind that dwells upon form and so forth, stating:
"One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere. Commentary: [As stated above.]
Next, the second section, "Re-establishing the Chinese Text," is further divided into two parts:
first, establishing it through positive reasoning, and second, refuting it through negation.
This is the former.
Once one dwells upon form and so forth, the mind arises and increases the suffering of saṃsāra,
such that one is unable to resolve to attain enlightenment.
If one wishes to resolve to attain enlightenment and transcend birth and death, [one must abandon these attachments].
Therefore, one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
The Sūtra says:
"If the mind has a dwelling, it is precisely non-dwelling. Commentary:
This is a refutation.
Since it was previously taught that one should not give rise to a mind directed toward form and so forth,
it is therefore exhorted that one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
It does not mean that one further abides in the mental state of non-abiding.
If there were a characteristic of abiding or non-abiding,
that too would be the arising of a mind, which is precisely non-abiding.
Because those who dwell in reality do not dwell at all;
and because those who do not dwell accord with the principle of reality.
This very principle of reality—
This is the bodhi of the Buddha.
If the mind dwells upon signs such as form and so forth,
that mind does not dwell in the bodhi of the Buddha.
[Sūtra]:
"Therefore, one should practice giving even with material things such as form (*rūpa*). [Commentary]:
This is the conclusion and the exhortation.
This is because one who dwells [in such things] does not possess patience. Therefore,
the Buddha previously stated that the minds of bodhisattvas should not dwell on form while practicing giving.
Since dwelling upon form and so forth is not true giving,
dwelling upon form and so forth is likewise not true patience;
therefore, the mind should be without any dwelling place.
[Sūtra]:
Subhūti, [this applies] up to such giving. [Commentary]:
Next, it is shown that among the causes and conditions for the suffering of sentient beings' opposition, [giving serves as the remedy].
The text consists of three parts:
first, the direct antidote;
second, causing [others] to believe and accept it.
Subsequently, attachment is abandoned.
This [process] further consists of two parts from the beginning:
first, the general presentation of the antidote.
This is the first [point] regarding the subsequent separate explanation of the reason why,
although they have resolved their minds, they do not abide in cyclic existence.
If there are sentient beings who oppose them, and when they forcibly give rise to patience amidst thoughts of suffering,
they immediately become weary and give rise to regression;
thus they are unable to constantly fulfill the bodhisattva’s resolve to practice giving and other such deeds.
Since the original purpose is to benefit all sentient beings,
one should not dwell upon the perception of sentient beings or the notion of opposition while practicing generosity;
when opposition arises, do not give rise to anger or resentment.
If one forcibly practices forbearance, regression will inevitably arise;
this is because such a state cannot abide in benefiting sentient beings,
and one must therefore distance oneself from all such appearances of phenomena.
The treatise composes a verse based on this:
One should recognize that the benefit of practice arises from such causes;
One should likewise know [the nature of] sentient beings and their objective characteristics, And how to remain detached from them.
Sūtra:
“The Tathāgata speaks of ‘sentient beings,’ yet they are not [truly] sentient beings. Commentary:
This is the specific explanation of the reason [for this statement].
The text consists of four phrases.
The first two phrases clarify the characteristic of non-self;
the latter two phrases clarify the characteristic of non-dharmas.
Because Bodhisattvas do not understand that sentient beings truly lack a self or dharmas, they hold views that are contradictory and harmful.
Now, in order to remedy this, the two absences [of self and dharmas] are taught;
once these contradictions are eliminated, [peace is attained].
It would be better to give rise to the perception of suffering.
Based on this meaning, the treatise composes a verse:
"The conventional designation and the aggregates— The Tathāgata is free from those characteristics."
The Buddhas do not possess those two, because they perceive the true Dharma.
To speak of "provisional names" is precisely the mark of a self;
since the mark of a self in sentient beings is merely a provisional name.
To speak of the "matters of the aggregates" (skandha-vastu) is precisely to speak of their "dharma-characteristics" (lakṣaṇa).
This is because the essential nature of the five aggregates constitutes their dharma-characteristics,
and because the Buddha has realized this through direct realization.
Because it is taught that the two [self-natures] are non-existent, they lack the characteristic of self;
because it is taught that all characteristics are in fact no-characteristics, there is no characteristic of dharmas;
and all sentient beings are in fact no-sentient-beings.
This interpretation of the sūtra accords with the intent of the śāstra.
The sūtra states:
"The Tathāgata does not speak otherwise. The commentary says:
This is to cause [them] to believe and accept it;
that is, to sever doubts regarding the ninth path as being a non-productive cause,

One practices patience by relying [on this].
Previously, it was stated that one should perform acts of worship based on the sūtras as a reliance, so that the fruit of merit may be accomplished;
when upholding and expounding the sūtras, one must remain free from laziness and endure hardships.
Because one should diligently uphold these marks of Buddhahood in order to swiftly attain Buddhahood,
it is said that one should practice the patience regarding the signless nature of dharmas such as non-self, and endure the suffering and other adversities caused by those sentient beings.
However, because these bodhisattvas have not yet abandoned their grasping mind,
they are unable to rely on the sūtras to practice the conduct of patience; thus,
they do not wish to believe or accept practices that depart from their own [preconceived] views.
I fear that this sutra may not be the true cause for Buddhahood. If,

this refers to the practice of the Four Noble Truths of the Hīnayāna.

Because this practice of the path to cessation is pure,

This refers to the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
It is because this is taught as the equal dharma of the Mahāyāna.
As for the phrase "not differing from one's words": it means that what is spoken does not contradict what is practiced.
Setting aside the discussion of ultimate truth,

Sūtra:

This is the refutation of attachment.
Because they have heard the previously mentioned true words and so forth,
although they give rise to faith and acceptance, this is called "clinging to the literal meaning," which conversely results in their own fault.
This reveals that although what the Buddha has taught is free from falsehood,
it nevertheless should not be grasped literally.
To negate and reveal this, it is said that [dharmas] lack reality and so forth.
That is to say, verbal expressions are merely conventional designations; dharmas are fundamentally beyond words, and words are not the dharmas themselves.
However, in accordance with that wisdom which realizes the truth:
because phenomena that can be grasped through words do not exist, it is not real;
because the dharma realized by wordless wisdom is not non-existent, it is not false.
Since phenomena are already beyond words and words are not the phenomena themselves, they lack substantial reality;
yet, because they can accord with and lead to the realization of wisdom, they are not false.
Based on this meaning, the treatise composes a verse:
In accordance with that true wisdom, it is taught as neither unreal nor real;
one realizes the truth by taking the sound as heard, and the sutra is spoken as an antidote to this.

Next, it reveals the cause and conditions for the suffering of enjoyment as an antidote;
that is, the severing of the tenth [affliction], which is the doubt regarding whether one has realized suchness or not.
This causes one to practice the patience of enduring suffering as it arises.
Although one has previously been led to abandon the perception of adverse suffering,
if the mind dwells on the notion that resources are lacking, [it will not be possible].
Furthermore, they do not apply themselves with diligence and frequently regress;
because their minds dwell on something and fail to accord with True Suchness (tathatā),
and because they harbor the notion of suffering, they instead doubt whether True Suchness is all-pervasive throughout time and space.
If a sage were to be designated by the name "True Suchness" (tathatā),
then since this exists at all times and in all places,
why is it that some people attain it while others do not?
As for those who realize the truth, how can they be said to attain stability by means of a mind that does not abide?
It is because one cannot [attain it] through abiding;
thus, although there is cultivation, there is realization.
Due to doubt, one does not cultivate the causes for the absence of suffering.
Now, wishing to sever that state of mind characterized by doubt,
one brings about the realization of suchness so as to give rise to true patience (*kṣānti*).
To say that the mind abides is to enter darkness and so forth;
Asaṅga, regarding this as causing non-abiding, calls it the "remedy for the perception of suffering from a lack of resources.
Vasubandhu, from the perspective of severing doubt, calls it "realizing suchness" rather than "not realizing."
Within the text concerning doubt, there are two parts:
first, the teaching and illustration clarifying that those lacking wisdom dwell in delusion;
second, the teaching and illustration clarifying that those possessing wisdom do not so dwell.
This is the first [point].
It means that within the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*), all myriad virtues are perfectly complete and non-abiding;
when internally realized, there is nothing whatsoever upon which to abide.
External mindfulness is the cause for that which is gone toward.
Because the minds of bodhisattvas abide in something and are defiled by ignorance,
they do not perceive suchness.
Consequently, one perceives a lack of resources in the present life and gives rise to the perception of suffering.
Since all spiritual practice seeks the fruit of future happiness,
if this were the case, would it not follow that there would be the perception of suffering regarding both the current lack and the future fruit as well?
True suchness does not perish;
since it truly pervades all times and places,
the wise do not abide [in it], because their minds are pure.
Because fools abide in the defilement of dharmas,
they cannot attain [realization]; it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing, for they do not perceive the truth.
Yet one sees that they are currently destitute;
how could they possibly escape suffering regarding their future results?
It is like that foolish person who casts himself into the darkness to search for an object, yet sees nothing at all.
Because one obtains [resources] that are deficient from beginning to end,
the mind dwells in attachment;
this is precisely what is to be remedied— the deficiency in the requisites for enjoyment, which should be abandoned.
Therefore, the *Vigrahavyāvartanī-kārikā* by Devaśarman states:
Time and place truly exist, yet true suchness is not attained;
Because of dwelling in dharmas through lack of wisdom, others likewise fail to attain it through lack of wisdom.
Sūtra:
"If a bodhisattva reaches the point of seeing various forms... Commentary:
This refers to the realization of wisdom that does not abide [in signs].
Regarding signs, this is precisely the practice that serves as the remedy.
If bodhisattvas do not dwell upon signs,
their minds will be purified, emerging from the night of ignorance.
They then realize the various virtuous functions of True Suchness (tathatā).
Since they are free from the marks of suffering in the present,
they do not seek future fruits for the acts of giving and so forth that they perform.
When one’s future fruits are never lacking, what suffering could there be?
It is like a wise person who possesses the eye of wisdom; when the sun of wisdom shines, they see all manner of things.
Using them according to what is seen, how could there ever be a lack from beginning to end? Thus, the mind abides nowhere.
Because this serves as an antidote,
bodhisattvas should remain without abiding anywhere,
yet they are able to give rise to true patience of acceptance (*kṣānti*), so that they do not conceive thoughts of deprivation regarding their enjoyments.
When practicing giving and other virtues, one seeks the fruit of future happiness.
Based on this meaning, the treatise states in verse:

"Regarding the Dharma" refers to the wisdom that acts as the antidote, which is like the eye and the sun.
The antidote is like the darkness that constitutes the obstacle to be countered;
one who attains the dharma of cessation realizes the principle of suchness, just as one sees various forms after the darkness has been dispelled.

having practiced the supreme conduct at that time,
