Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed the prediction upon me,
for it would have already been attained at that time.
Śākyamuni is translated here as "Able to Pacify."
Because one who is already able to bring peace to oneself is also able to bring peace to others, the Sūtra says:
"In reality, there is none [who attains it]... up to Śākyamuni. The commentary states:
This is what is established here.
For truly there are no superior practices to be performed,
nor is there any enlightenment to be realized as it is described in words.
Furthermore, at that time, my mind attained nothing and my conduct accorded with principle;
since there was no retrogression,
Dīpaṃkara therefore bestowed upon me the prophecy of my future enlightenment.
The verse of the treatise says:
Because he received the prediction for a later time, the practice under Dīpaṃkara was not the supreme enlightenment;
those practices were equal [to it], yet they do not possess the characteristics of truly existent conditioned phenomena.
[Sūtra]: Why is this?
It reaches the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. [Commentary]:
This true suchness (*bhūtatathatā*) is ineffable.
The text investigates and explains:
For what reason is there no real dharma in bodhi?
If there is no bodhi, then the Buddha also does not exist.
As for the statement that nothing can be apprehended at that time,
why is this so? It is because that which was bestowed as a prophecy of Tathāgata-hood at that time—
The Tathāgata is the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena;
yet this suchness is truly ineffable,
for it is free from the mental agitation of conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and outflows (*āsrava*) are not of a different nature,
at that time there is neither speaking nor attaining;
thus says the Sūtra.
If someone were to say that [the Buddha] attains up to *samyak-saṃbodhi*, the commentary states:
"This Buddha does not attain *bodhi*.
Within this text, two types of responses are given to refute and dispel such attachments.
If someone were to say that at the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, because their causal practice was not supreme,
they did not attain bodhi; yet later, when they became a Buddha, their resultant virtue was extraordinary—
would there then be some real dharma by which one attains perfect enlightenment?

Therefore, the correct refutation states that not only was enlightenment not attained at that time, but even when he later became a Buddha, it was likewise because, according to the practice of the cause, there was truly nothing to be attained.
As the previous verse stated: "Enlightenment, those practices," and so forth.
[Sūtra]:
"Subhūti, it is neither real nor unreal. [Commentary]:
This refutes the attachments to both increase and decrease.
Fearing that upon hearing of cause and effect they might believe in non-attainment,
they would then slander the Tathāgata, claiming that there is no bodhi at all,
asserting that what is called "bodhi" is entirely false and merely a fabrication for the sake of exclusion.
For this reason, it is said that they are unreal and empty.
The Buddha’s bodhi is precisely suchness (tathatā).
True Suchness (tathatā) possesses neither falsehood nor reality.
There is one reality and two aspects; because the reality lacks the conceptualized marks of the five aggregates of conditioned existence, it is said to be without reality.

The preceding verse states: "It is not that the characteristics of conditioned phenomena do not truly exist; because the worldly path of realization and cultivation possesses the true characteristics of reality, it is said to be non-deceptive.
Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"That which is non-characteristic is itself the characteristic; this is spoken of as being non-false.
Thus says the Sūtra.
Therefore, "all that the Tathāgata has attained is the Buddha-dharma. The commentary states:
This suchness (tathatā) pervades all phenomena,
because the aforementioned bodhi is suchness.
Suchness is the very essence of the Honored Buddha and is also the dharma realized by all Buddhas.
Suchness universally constitutes the nature of all phenomena;
it is the dharma of all Buddhas and the essential characteristic of all things.
The Buddha has no attainment by which he can attain this Dharma;
the Bodhisattva, likewise, should attain it through non-attainment. Sūtra.
"Subhūti, this is called 'all dharmas'. The commentary says:
This establishes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because previously it was shown that suchness (*tathatā*) pervades all dharmas.
All phenomena are the Buddha-dharma.
[This is said] because one fears that others might falsely cling to the distinction between subject and object, or to separate phenomena such as form and so forth,
and take them to be the Buddha-dharma.
The statement "now I send forth these words" and so on refers to the fact that all that is spoken is the Buddha-dharma;
this is because one has realized *tathatā* (suchness) through the non-apprehension of any object.
Because one can perceive forms and so forth without falling into partiality,
it is said that all things are the Buddha-dharma;
this is not a false arising.
All that is distinguished by the mind of grasping is called the Buddha-dharma.
If one is free from the mind that distinguishes between subject and object, then observing form is observing the truth, and observing the truth is observing form.
"All dharmas are called the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, having received the Buddha's instruction,
I came to know that all dharmas are indeed the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, they were granted the prediction that they would attain Buddhahood.
For this reason, all bodhisattvas also seek instruction in order to awaken to all Buddha-dharmas and swiftly achieve the fruit of Buddhahood.
Although Śākyamuni encountered many Buddhas in the past, he mentions only Dīpaṃkara as an example.
This sutra takes non-characteristic (*animitta*) as its primary tenet.

At the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, [the Bodhisattva] realized and testified to this through myriad means; having practiced for ten thousand kalpas, he entered the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Therefore, the phrases within this section specifically highlight this point.
Sūtra:
"Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body was tall and large. Commentary:
This has already revealed the stage of faith and understanding prior to the [first] bhūmi and the eighth bhūmi.
Next, the second section below clarifies the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*),
which is the seventeenth dwelling place of realized practice (*pratipannamārgasthāna*).
Vasubandhu’s commentary explains this through metaphors to clarify the doubts [regarding it].
They enter equally into the true vision.
For those bodhisattvas who previously practiced through faith, he taught the four kinds of sublime practices prior to the stages;
there is no place where they do not universally deliver beings.
There is no practice that is not universal;
there is no cultivation without fruit that is not universal; there is no aspect of non-obstruction that is not universal.
Thus, the practices of the Four Great Vows have been fully manifested.
Regarding the former two [truths], the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*) was about to open;
regarding the latter, it is now missing from the exposition.
Thus, the arising of this text constitutes a deficiency in the teaching of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which consists of the principle and wisdom (*jñāna*).
This causes these bodhisattvas to manifest the specific lower obstacles and give rise to the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*),
thereby personally realizing and experiencing it;
yet, because these bodhisattvas do not depart from the specific lower minds they have attained.
Although he has heard the preceding teaching and realized the true Dharma-body through non-apprehension,
his doubts have not yet been fully dispelled.
Fearing that one might think the Dharma-body is also something to be attained,
he then uses a metaphor to clarify it,
thereby resolving the doubt.
It is said, for example, that the body becomes large and so forth;
Asaṅga, referring to the principle and wisdom illustrated by these metaphors,
speaks of the pure mind realizing the path.
Vasubandhu employs an analogy to clarify the preceding doubt; thus, it is called "an exposition by way of analogy that clarifies doubt.
The text below is divided into two parts:
first, the attainment of wisdom is made manifest.
The latter [section] on abandoning pride leads to realization;
the former [section] also has two parts:
first, the teaching by means of the analogy of the Tathāgata, and second, the confirmation through Subhūti’s response.
This is the first point.
The principle of true suchness (tathatā) is realized only through internal verification; its essence cannot be designated by means of words or conceptual characteristics.
Nevertheless, because those who possess wisdom attain clarity through analogies, [the following is said].
Next, the "Great Body" is used to penetrate the profound essence.
For example, when one praises the fullness of a person's physical features and gathers their virtuous appearance,
this is collectively termed the "Great Body."
The wisdom and insight realized therein is called "Dharma.
Because it encompasses and achieves [all qualities], it is called "Body" (kāya).
Thus, this Dharmakāya is named the "Great and Long" (Mahāpuruṣa).
This refers to the Dharmakāya manifested through the realization of the path of entry,
because it is manifested by the attainment of two types of knowledge.
Regarding what is called the "attainment of the two types of knowledge":
First is the wisdom that encompasses the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, one attains this wisdom and is born into the family of the Tathāgata.
They firmly establish the seed of the Buddha.
Having previously been born into this family throughout the long night,
once they have attained birth, they are ultimately bound to its basis and are thus able to attain the realization and fulfillment thereof.
Because his wondrous body possesses the three marks of merit, he is called "Long Body.
The three marks of merit refer to the three wondrous fruits of retribution, response, and transformation.
Second, regarding the joy of directness: beginning from the first stage (bhūmi), one is able to realize the five kinds of equality.
One accomplishes the wisdom of equality.
Regarding the five equalities:
first, the wisdom of realization through the equality of severing evil, because one does not perceive any distinction between suffering and pleasure.
1. The wisdom of realization that perceives no distinction between self and other through the equality of the two types of selflessness and their karmic activities; 2.
The wisdom of realization of the equality of correspondence that perceives no distinction between self and others; 3.
The wisdom of realization of the equality of the aspiration-free mind that benefits others without seeking recompense.
Because all Bodhisattvas realize the equality of the path and thereby can give rise to the wisdom of identical essence (*sārabhāva-jñāna*),
they universally gather in all sentient beings once this wisdom is attained.
Because it is that which gathers in the body [of all beings], it is called the "Great Body" (*mahākāya*).
Since this wisdom is obtained through the realization of the Path,
it is hereafter designated as "grown" in reference to the Dharmakāya;
how much more so when the Dharmakāya manifested at the stage of ultimate fruition transcends all objective domains.
Pervading all objects and possessing a body of great merit, it is most excellently termed "vast.
Therefore, the treatise, referring to the resultant *dharmakāya*, states in verse:
"Relying upon that *dharmakāya* Buddha, The metaphor of the 'great body' is taught."
The body is free from all obstructions and possesses the merit of pervading all objects;
because it is of such a great essence, it is called the "Great Body.
Since that which is not a body is precisely the mind, it is therefore called "not a body."
The first two lines explain the meaning of the metaphor;
the last two lines interpret the subsequent scriptural passage;
and the four intermediate lines correctly elucidate this principle.
[Sūtra]:
Subhūti said: "...this is called the 'Great Body'. [Commentary]:
This is the present answer that establishes [the point].
The Tathāgata has taught that the body is "great" because it is established as being without the characteristics of self or other.
If there were distinct characteristics of self and other within the body, [it would not be great].
That would then not be a "great body. If,
apart from these distinct characteristics, there exists that true suchness which is the characteristic of the same essence,
this is called a "great body."
Therefore, the preceding verse states that "that which is not the body is itself the body.
Thus, it speaks of "non-body," because within that body,
the characteristics of being neither self nor other are established.
Sūtra:
Subhūti, a bodhisattva who has reached [this state] is not called a "bodhisattva. Commentary:
Next follows the thirteenth doubt, which clarifies the realization through the elimination of pride.
Because from the first bhūmi one abandons the pride of "I" and attains the two types of knowledge,
up until the attainment of Buddhahood, one is able to manifest the pure and wondrous Great Dharmakāya.
Desiring to cause those who practice with faith to fulfill their bodhisattva path and swiftly enter the path of realization to achieve awakening, it is called the "Great and Vast Body."
They cause one to take as the realization of the essence a mind free from the marks of self and other-egoism;
yet because bodhisattvas are unable to realize the Path without abandoning conceit,
they conversely doubt non-self.
Then there would be no bodhisattvas;
and if there were no bodhisattvas, there would likewise be no Buddhas,
even though they deliver sentient beings and adorn and purify buddha-fields.
If this were so, why would one need to resolve to practice the path and seek the Dharma-body?
It is because of pride that one lacks wisdom and does not realize the Way.
Because of doubt, there is conceit, and one does not accord with reality.
Now, wishing to reveal that mind of doubt and conceit, it is said:
"One should be like the Bodhisattva Pure Mind, who, free from afflictions, inversions, and conceit, has accomplished the wondrous great body."
Asaṅga, focusing on the obstacles of pride and attachment, speaks of "leaving behind pride" to bring about realization;
Vasubandhu, focusing on the removal of doubt, speaks of "manifesting the practice" so that one does not harbor doubts regarding Buddhahood.
The text below is divided into four parts.
This is the first [section], which announces the grounds for the accusation and resolves the doubt.
It is because one harbors arrogance within the false mind, despite the fact that [the afflictions] necessarily do not pervade the *tathatā-dharmadhātu*.
That is to say, because they have heard it said that in reality there is no such thing as a bodhisattva,
they instead doubt whether their practice is correct;
thus, they achieve nothing at all.
If doubt and pride arise, how can one accomplish the practice?
For it is through attaining wisdom and abandoning pride— free from the notion of "I" and "mine"— that the Buddhas and others grow their great bodies,
adorn the lands, and deliver sentient beings, thereby achieving spontaneous perfection.
Thus, because the bodhisattva is also equal to the Buddha in being free from pride, realizing the truth, and perfecting the great body,
it is said that "the bodhisattva is also like this.
If one thinks, "I shall deliver sentient beings," [one falls into conceit].
Because of the knowledge of "self," how could this inversion of self-conceit possibly attain the wisdom that encompasses the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) by means of perceiving sentient beings?
How can one who is deluded and inverted regarding others attain the wisdom of the equality of castes?
Since such wisdom cannot be attained due to pride and other afflictions,
there is no sublime and great body.
What is meant by "bodhisattva"?
Therefore, a verse in the treatise says:
Failing to realize the true dharma-realm, One gives rise to the intention to deliver sentient beings.
And regarding the purification of Buddha-fields, the very arising of such a thought is a perverted teaching.
Why is this? The commentary says:
This inquiry is not the proper reason.
The Sūtra says:
“Subhūti... up to being called a Bodhisattva. The Commentary says:
This is the basis for the explanation of its meaning:
because, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is formed by grasping the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);
whereas, according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is entirely devoid of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).
Whether mundane or ultimate,
what single dharma exists that can be called a "bodhisattva"?
Relying on what, then, could one give rise to pride and say, "I shall deliver them"?
[Sūtra]:
"Therefore, the Buddha taught up to 'the absence of a life-principle' (*jīva*). [Commentary]:
This concludes that all phenomena are without distinction; it is not only that for Bodhisattvas there is no such thing as a real, differentiated dharma.
I clearly understand that all dharmas are likewise so;
because both the person and the dharma, as well as the two vehicles, are non-existent,
and since both the person and the dharma are empty, one should not give rise to conceptualization.
If one does not exhaustively bring about this assembly of sentient beings,
then one cannot achieve the wondrous body or the great body;
for this reason, one cannot be called a bodhisattva.
That is to say, when one enters the path of seeing from the first bhūmi,
being free from the specific pride of superiority is called the "purified mind.
When the mind is purified and wisdom is attained, it is called the "path of realization."
Although the sutra extensively clarifies the practice of pure conduct (*śuddhacaryā*) and the stages of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*),
it briefly explains the pure mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) but does not clarify the pure mind realized in the ten stages.
This is because the primary intent of the sutra is to clarify the Buddha-lineage (*tathāgatagotra*) rather than to manifest the fruit of Buddhahood (*buddhatva-bodhi*).
This is the generation of the mind that succeeds [the Buddha].
Knowing that this is capable of succeeding [the Buddha], one raises up the fruit and seeks to extensively clarify the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*).
Although one cultivates and trains in the vast body prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), [this is the point of succession].
If one enters the path of seeing, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are naturally fulfilled and the fruit of Buddhahood is attained;
because the seeds [of these stages] are not explicitly manifested, the ten stages are mentioned briefly rather than explained in detail.
For this reason, it is called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Because there are differences in width and narrowness at the beginning, end, and middle. Sūtra:
“Subhūti, up to [the point where one] is not called a bodhisattva. Commentary says:
The second stage, the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*), has been explained above.
Next, the third stage, the Manifestation of the Tathāgata Ground (*tathāgataviṣayaprakāśanabhūmi*), follows;
this is the sixth among the eight ultimate abodes within the eighteen [grounds] for seeking the Buddha-ground above.
The preceding sections clarified the stages prior to the ground (*bhūmi*) and the subsequent stages of the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*).
Now, in order to inspire aspiration for the goal,
this section distinguishes the qualities of the fruition by enumerating the sixfold perfections of the Buddha-body.
It causes Bodhisattvas on the ten stages to seek upward;
based on the person who seeks, this is called "seeking upward for the abode of the Buddha-ground," and in terms of the fruit sought, it is called "ultimate."
Furthermore, the sixfold fulfillment of the Tathāgata stage is to be correlated as previously arranged;
this collectively reveals the two types of grasping— the environment and the body— of the Buddha-fruit,
for the Buddha-fruit necessarily possesses both the dependent and the primary retribution.
The first is the retributive environment (*niśraya-vipāka*),
and the latter five are the retributive bodies (*ātmabhāva-vipāka*).
To establish the retributive environment, the Pure Land is explained first.
Among the primary retributions, the three karmas must necessarily be guided by cognition;
therefore, clear knowledge and vision are presented first.
Among the three karmas, the body is that upon which they depend; therefore, it is mentioned next.
First, the primary marks and secondary signs are clarified.

These two sets of marks serve as manifestations of virtue, causing people to revere his virtues and assemble before him; the primary marks adorn his body, causing people to cherish and long for him, thereby leading them to draw near for the sake of benefiting others—this being the most excellent among such benefits.
First, the excellent physical marks are clarified because they constitute an excellent basis;
subsequently, the excellence of speech for the benefit of others is revealed;
and first, the mind is clarified because it is the foundation for benefiting others.
To provide an analysis for what follows, first, regarding the perfection of the purity of the buddha-field:
this refers to the practice of cultivating the activities for the fulfillment of the Buddha-fruit within the field that precedes the manifestation [of the result], so as to eliminate all doubts.
The text is divided into four parts:
first, citing the attachment to demonstrate its falsity;
second, investigating the reason for its falsity.
Third, the explicit manifestation of the adornment of the land;
fourth, the conclusion regarding the true bodhisattva.
This is the first [of these].

If a bodhisattva seeks the fruit of Buddhahood, they should rely on the correct practice of signless concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*) to eliminate those two attachments and thereby create true adornment.
If one says, "I shall [adorn] it," this is the attachment to a person (*pudgala-grāha*);
if one says, "it is for me," this is the attachment to dharmas (*dharma-grāha*). These constitute the adornment of the Buddha-land.
Once these two attachments have arisen, one does not realize the truth;
thus, the mind is not pure.
How, then, could it adorn the land?
To say "I shall adorn" is not the way of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, the preceding verse states:
"Even to give rise to the thought of purifying buddha-fields is itself a perversion."
[Sutra]:
Why is this? [Commentary]:
The objection raised here is not appropriate.
[Sūtra]:
"Adorning the Buddha-lands... this is called adorning. [Commentary]:
This correctly elucidates the adornment of the lands.
In this regard, if one wishes to truly adorn the land,
it is not by means of the characteristics of subject and object as adornments;
if one is free from subject and object, there is adornment without characteristics.
This is called adornment;
because it is true adornment,
one is able to fully realize the four bodies and the pure lands.
Therefore, this section is titled "The Perfection of the Land.

While the preceding sections dealt with the preliminary stages and the minor path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the present section establishes the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth as being fully perfected; thus, the text appears repetitive.
This differs from what was stated previously.
The Sūtra says:
"If a bodhisattva penetrates ultimate reality, he is a bodhisattva. The Commentary states:
This person is a true bodhisattva.
Because they do not say "I am able," they have realized that birth is empty and that there are no marks to adorn;
because they have realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*), the Tathāgata declares them to be a true bodhisattva.
The verse of the treatise says:
Sentient beings and bodhisattvas know that all phenomena are selfless;
The non-saints know through faith, And the saints know through direct realization.
A true bodhisattva is able to know that both their own body and the bodies of sentient beings are entirely devoid of a self;
this is not the case for an unenlightened bodhisattva,
who should instead rely on their own wisdom to have faith in the dharma of non-self.
Next, regarding the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*), is it because there is noble knowledge that one does not attain thorough penetration?
This indicates that those who possess grasping and fail to realize the two kinds of emptiness are not true Bodhisattvas.
[From] the Sūtra:
"Subhūti, does he possess even the fleshly eye? Commentary:
Next follows the second [section], the perfection of the purity of unsurpassed vision and knowledge.
This reveals the fourteenth [quality], the Buddha’s incapability of being seen, which causes one to seek the perfection of knowledge and vision in accordance with reality.
Previously, it was instructed that one should seek the Buddha’s *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive support) pure land.
The substance of this land encompasses both the sentient and the insentient;
it is composed of the seven treasures, which serve as the actual basis for the Bodhisattva’s activities and transformations.
This is what is enjoyed;
the sentient beings therein are those to be transformed and benefited.
If there were no knowledge or vision, who would undergo transformation?
Therefore, it is said that only through the purity of the five types of cultivation based on vision and the purity of the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) together with their supporting merit,
can one fully comprehend and utilize both the material and the immaterial.
They also know the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings and provide them with benefit and aid.
They are also able to lead others through inexhaustible means to constant peace and joy, transforming and guiding them.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas are resolutely intent on seeking the unsurpassed vision and wisdom of a Buddha.
Having heard what was previously stated— that not seeing any phenomena is called being a Buddha—
one might consequently doubt whether the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom of vision.
Now, by explaining that the Buddha is fully endowed with the wisdom of vision, this doubt is removed, and one now joyfully seeks to proceed toward that goal.
Asaṅga explains it in terms of the fruit sought, such that when vision and knowledge are fully attained, one is called a Buddha;
Vasubandhu explains it in terms of manifesting doubt regarding what is currently sought, stating that there is no one capable of seeing such doubt.
The section on the letter *ma* is divided into three parts.
First, it clarifies the perfection of the purity of vision;
next, it clarifies the perfection of the purity of wisdom.
Subsequently, the perfection of merit is revealed.
To discern and illuminate is called "vision" (darśana);
once this has been revealed, it is called "knowledge" (jñāna).
That which is lovely is called "merit" (*puṇya*).
Being free from obstructions and perfectly luminous is called "perfection of purity.
The five pure eyes (*pañca-cakṣuḥ*) seen therein constitute the five [eyes] mentioned below.
Each of these further consists of two parts:
first the question, and then the answer.
This is the first.

Question: The fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is so called because it breaks through the skin and the four sense-objects (*viṣaya*). It is named "eye" based on its pure fivefold retribution (*pañca-vipāka*).
If various vows have not yet attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), with the exception of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin-rāja*), [it does not arise].

One perceives only the forms within the internal obscuration of ignorance regarding the signs of desire in the immediate vicinity; these can only be fully accomplished when one is free from the obscuration of karmic retribution.
This is because Bodhisattvas take this body and mind as their own guide.
Regarding those who see sentient beings,
because they give rise to compassion,
they first cultivate and accomplish it.
Nevertheless, according to the capacity of the observer, one may see [the world] for a hundred yojanas up to the great trichiliocosm;
however, because of obstructions, one does not see other directions.
If it pertains to the Buddha-body, form is itself wisdom and principle is itself phenomena.
One is all, because one perceives the dharmadhātu as being without obstruction.

Because this is the vision of the retribution of pure, untainted form and the virtuous retribution that benefits others, it is called "fleshly vision" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) even though it is limited by the physical body.
Now, wishing to reveal that the Buddha possesses this purity of vision, he asks Subhūti: "Does the Tathāgata exist?
(Sūtra)
"In this way, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, possesses the fleshly eye.
Commentary: This is the answer.
The Buddha, having transcended all hindrances, is able to benefit himself and others; in these five respects, he is equal to ordinary beings.
The fifth is the pure, untainted physical eye produced [by karma].
If this were absent, one would not be complete;
thus says the Sūtra.
"Does Subhūti possess the divine eye? [The commentary] states:
This question concerns the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
First, it raises the term "pure meditative absorption" (*śuddhadhyāna*) and designates it as "heaven" (*deva*).
It is called the "divine eye" (divyacakṣus) because it illuminates by means of the heavens.
Furthermore, this divine eye is obtained either through karmic retribution or through cultivation.
If it is induced in accordance with the dhyānas as a pure form-substance (*rūpa*) that has been exhausted within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is termed "obtained through cultivation."
If one is born among the devas, the pure matter produced by karmic causes, which is designated as "vision," is called "attained through retribution.
These two types of divine vision and hearing can perceive objects at a distance; however, regarding external forms, their respective spheres of perception are proximate.
There is indeed a distinction:
if one attains this through aspiration, one sees the four continents, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas;
gradually, from small to large, one sees the forms of the small, medium, and great trichiliocosms.
In order to abandon the aforementioned defects of the fleshly eye and to wish to know the six realms of existence,
Bodhisattvas cultivate the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) as described in various treatises;
at its minimum, it can see a hundred *yojanas*.
Furthermore, they see as far as the greatest extent of the worlds of the ten directions—
forms invisible even to the devas and those of the two vehicles—
and they perceive the causes and effects of defilement and purity throughout the three periods of time.
If it resides within the Buddha-body,
it is the true divine eye, for it perceives all things without dualistic characteristics.
Now, [the text] seeks to demonstrate that the Buddha possesses this purity of vision.
Question: "Subhūti, does the Tathāgata exist?
Sūtra: "In this way, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye. Commentary: It says:
This is the answer:
because the Buddha, having fully perfected the cultivation of detachment in the past,
constantly abides in samādhi regarding his present fruits and virtues.
Able to benefit oneself and others by contemplating inexhaustible objects;
this is the true divine eye obtained through retribution and cultivation.
Subhūti possesses even the eye of wisdom. Commentary:
This question concerns the "eye of wisdom.
To distinguish and explain the terms "defilement" and "purity" is called wisdom;
that which can illuminate ultimate truth is called the eye.
The noble beings of the three vehicles take the wisdom that realizes the two kinds of emptiness as their eye of prajñā.
The aforementioned divine eye has not yet transcended the false and illusory;
therefore, bodhisattvas, desiring to know the true nature of all phenomena and to accomplish reality, emerge from the path of birth and death.
Furthermore, for those who wish to be free from falsehood in this very life, in order to provide them with rescue and relief, they next cultivate the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
Upon reaching the Buddha-body, the one is identical to all; by means of a single gnosis (*jñāna*), one perceives that which penetrates both principle and phenomena.
From the perspective of illuminating the principle (*tattva*), it is also called the "eye of wisdom" (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
Now, in order to reveal this very point, the Sūtra asks whether it exists or not.
"In this way, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, possesses the eye of wisdom. The commentary states:
This is the answer.

Because the Buddha is free from marks (*animitta*), he contemplates form as being like clouds and universally realizes the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses the eye of grace.
Sūtra:
Subhūti, up to the point of possessing the Dharma-eye. Commentary:
This question concerns the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).
The retributive nature of sentient beings is called "Dharma" because it accords with reality;
the subsequent wisdom that illuminates and penetrates it is called the "eye."
The Mahāyāna cause and effect illuminate the two kinds of emptiness;
through this, one is further able to give rise to subsequent conventional wisdom,
which can know the differences in the nature of the retributions of sentient beings.
Furthermore, that which can illuminate and comprehend dharmas such as names and phrases—
contrary to the dharmas being observed— is called the Dharma-eye.
If there were only the wisdom-eye, one would have no knowledge of dharmas.
Thus, unlike the two vehicles which cannot universally benefit others,
the Bodhisattva cultivates the Dharma-eye in order to know the retributions of sentient beings and to apply the methods for delivering them.
If one reaches the level of the Buddha’s body, although it directly illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
from the perspective of attaining the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), it may also be called "existent.
It is for the purpose of clarifying this present point that the question is raised.
Sūtra:
"In this way, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye.
Commentary: This is the answer.
Since the Buddha has realized the truth and attained thorough penetration of all dharmas,
what object of desire could he not comprehend?
What name or phrase could he not know?
The supreme means for benefiting others is the Dharma-eye.
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, does one possess the Buddha-eye?"
The commentary states:
This question concerns the Buddha-eye.
Because his realization of the Way is perfect and complete, he is called a Buddha.
It is called the "eye" because it universally observes principles and phenomena.
There are two kinds of the Buddha-eye:
first, the general; second, the specific.
In general, this refers to the synthesis of the four aforementioned eyes;
just as the confluence of four rivers forms a total mass called an ocean,
so too is this aggregate named the "ocean."
The "distinct" refers to the Buddha-body,
which has the non-conceptual wisdom of all modes as its essential nature.
The preceding four eyes are distinguished by their names.

Because in the causal stage one has not yet attained penetration, is not free from hindrances, and one's vision of objects is not yet all-encompassing, one’s self-benefit and benefit for others remain inferior;
therefore, in order to make these perfect and supreme, one cultivates the Buddha-eye.
Now, as one is about to manifest Buddhahood, one does so in order to purify this vision.
First, it asks whether the Tathāgata exists or not.
The Sūtra says:
"In this way, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye. The commentary states:
This is the answer.
Because it transcends the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) and universally manifests the non-obstruction and mutual fusion of principle and phenomena (*li-shi*), there is the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*).
In the preceding texts concerning the various stages (*vihāra*), the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) was not established.
These all speak of existence and do not speak of non-existence;
since this [text] and the *Jingzheng lun* (Treatise on the Purity of Wisdom) both dwell together in the same location, the latter clarifies the former, and thus they share the same interpretation.
Sūtra:
Subhūti, when it is said that this is "purity of wisdom" (*jñāna-viśuddhi*), the commentary states:
"The following clarifies purity of wisdom.
The preceding 'purity of vision' (*darśana-viśuddhi*) was able to illuminate the essence of wisdom."
This purity of wisdom is able to illuminate the function of wisdom because the essence and its function are distinct;
in the two lower stages of non-attachment, the function does not depart from the essence.
Vasubandhu’s unification of these is precisely due to the fact that through the purity of vision, one is able to give rise to pure wisdom.
Having already explained the distinctions in the mental activities of sentient beings,
one causes their minds to be free from all distraction and to realize the true realm;
therefore, it is called the "Pure Abiding of Wisdom."
The passage below is divided into three parts.
First, it presents what wisdom is capable of;
second, it clarifies that the Buddha is capable of knowing.
The subsequent section investigates and explains the reason for this.
The first part, in turn, has four sections.
The first distinguishes the sand by means of the river.
Second, the realm of the number of sands due to causes;
third, the explanation of arising due to causes and effects;
fourth, the explanation of mind due to arising from causes.
This is the first [point].
Because the Tathāgata, relying on conventional truth, wishes to manifest the vast number of matters concerning the principle of wisdom and the mind of consciousness, he spoke thus:
"This arises from faith; it is empty and its retribution is boundless."
[Sūtra]:
Subhūti, would that be much? [Commentary]: This refers to world-systems as numerous as the sands [of the Ganges].
As stated in the *Awakening of Faith*: "Because space is boundless, the realms are boundless.
[From the] Sūtra:
The Buddha addressed Subhūti... up to "all sentient beings. Commentary:
This discourse on cause and effect explains arising.
It is also as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*:
because the world is boundless, sentient beings are boundless.
Sūtra: "Various kinds of mind. Commentary:
This is spoken in terms of the arising of the cause.
Furthermore, just as sentient beings are infinite, so too are the distinctions in their mental activities infinite.
Regarding the various types, one should know that they are further categorized into two kinds.
The first is the defiled mind; that is,
the mind characterized by common desire belonging to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*),
because such a mind is unable to cultivate the first four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
First, regarding the essence of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, one falsely clings to it as permanent, blissful, and self, thereby giving rise to attachment and protection.
Second is the pure mind;
that is, the mind free from desire toward these two types of self.
Because they are unable to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness,
they erroneously cling to their own buddha-nature— which is the true essence of permanence, bliss, self, and purity— as being impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure.
Because they seek transcendence,

the *Dharmatr̥pti-śāstra* (Tianqin lun) states that while the true foundations of mindfulness (*smr̥tyupasthāna*) are termed "permanently abiding and immovable," their fundamental names differ in meaning;
since both are explained as being the true Dharma, there are two kinds of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Sūtra:
"The Tathāgata knows them all. Commentary:
The above clarifies the objects of cognition.
This reveals that which is capable of knowing.
There are two kinds of knowing:
first, knowing both the defiled and the pure in their entirety.
Second, because one knows that both defilement and purity are entirely inverted,
a verse in the treatise says:
"Though one does not perceive any phenomena, it is not that there is no eye that cognizes objects."
Because one perceives those inversions—
various inverted cognitions that are devoid of true mindfulness and do not abide in true wisdom—
it is therefore called the "Sūtra on Inversion."
Why is this so? The commentary states:
This section explains the reason for it, and therein there are four parts.
This is the first instance of a question and answer used for investigation and explanation.
It is not only that objects are numerous, but the mind is also difficult to perceive.
Why is it that one is able to know them all?
The Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgata speaks of all minds; this is what is called 'mind'. The Commentary says:
This is the answer.
When the Tathāgata speaks of these various minds of defilement and purity,
from the perspective of conventional truth, they are for the most part not minds that abide in the four foundations of mindfulness.
Because within the gateway of ultimate truth, neither a mind that dwells nor a mind that does not dwell can be apprehended;
it is only in conventional truth that defilement and purity are designated as mere provisional names.
If the inverted mind grasps at the characteristics of the mind, it will give rise to obstruction alone.
One cannot know even a single thought-moment; yet,
by seeing that all thoughts are not non-thoughts,
one attains the true principle and is thus able to know them all.
This is identical to what is taught in the *Awakening of Faith*; one should cite it there.
The Sūtra asks: "Why is this so? The Commentary says:
This is an inquiry.
Since it has been stated that this is mind, yet also stated that it is not mind,
for what reason is this so?
Sūtra:
"The past mind is ultimately unattainable. Commentary:
This is the explanation.
However, the mind can transform objects,
and objects in turn give rise to the mind;
thus, mind and object arise through mutual dependence, forming the characteristic of conditionality.
If it takes a past object as its condition, it is called a past mind;
if it contemplates a future object, it is called a future mind;
if it grasps a present object, it is called a present mind.
Since the objects of the three periods of time are already detached from the mind, there is no cessation or arising;
because delusion has no abiding place, the minds of the three periods—whether already ceased or yet to arise—are likewise delusory and have no abiding place.
Because all are unattainable,
the sūtra says that all minds are "non-minds."
"Subhūti, will he obtain much merit? [The commentary] states:
Within the purification of wisdom and vision, merit is fully perfected;
this reveals that the fifteenth [topic], merit, is not to be doubted as being unwholesome.
It causes one to cultivate the Buddha-body, which is fully endowed with merit and wisdom;
for merit serves as the guide that generates further fortune,
and merit acts as the basis that can support wisdom.
If one lacks merit, what can knowledge and vision rely upon?
Being unable to dwell in the pure lands mentioned before,
nor being able to bring about the subsequent signs for the formation of the two bodies.
Regarding the provisional and ultimate merits of the past and future, all bodhisattvas are unable to comprehend the mind;
because they are all non-minds that are free from inversion,
they instead doubt that merit itself is also free from inversion.
One might raise this doubt:
"If it is said that both defiled and pure minds are inverted,
then practicing merit based on the mind would also be a departure from inversion."
Since it is not wholesome, why would one need to practice it?
Because of dogmatic adherence, one does not abandon the causes of perversion;
because of doubt, one does not cultivate the merit that abandons perversion.
Now, wishing to reveal that mind of doubt and attachment so that practitioners may cultivate merit free from inversion,
it is shown that merit free from signs is exceedingly vast.
Asaṅga explains that practicing merit while remaining free from attachment is called "endowment with merit.
Vasubandhu dispels doubts by knowing what is wholesome; this clarifies that the doubt regarding merit is not itself wholesome.
The following text consists of three question-and-answer sections concerning its establishment.
This is the first.
With a mind free from inversion and non-abiding,
one offers the seven treasures as a gift to the Tathāgata.
"One shall attain the sovereignty of merit and virtue of a Buddha's body.
By this causal condition, would not one's merit be great? Thus it is said in the Sūtra.
"In this way, World-Honored One, one attains exceedingly great merit.
The commentary says:
This is the answer, given by means of such conditions for non-abiding giving.
When one perceives the Buddha-body, the merit is exceedingly great.
Sūtra: Subhūti, [the merit] attained is very much. Commentary: It is said:
This explains the establishment [of the point].
If one dwells in the three spheres with a mind that grasps at merit as being real,
since that is inverted, the merit will be limited.
One does not say that the merit is great;
rather, the merit cultivated with a signless mind can serve as the foundation for the wisdom of a Buddha.
This is because it is not a merit based on the inversion of abiding in existence;
rather, it is because my, the Tathāgata’s, merit is vast.
As a verse in the treatise says:
The root of the Buddha’s wisdom is the merit of non-perversion;
because of these characteristics of merit, this Sūtra of Parables is spoken again.
"Subhūti, [he is] endowed with a complete form-body. The commentary states:
Next follows the third section, the perfection of the body of secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), which clarifies the sixteenth mark of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*) and resolves doubts regarding the Buddha.
This causes one to cultivate the perfection of the Buddha-body.
Having previously studied the purification of the Buddha-fields through bodily action and cultivated superior wisdom and vision to discern both principle and phenomena,
one next adorns all the primary and secondary marks of the Buddha.
However, the Buddha’s marks and signs arise from the Dharma-body;
their true virtues are limitless and their marks and signs are boundless,
all pervading the Dharma-realm just as the true essence itself does.
For this reason, it is called being "endowed with the marks and signs.
Therefore, when it is said that the body does not possess an infinite variety of colors and so forth,
one should contemplate the *dharmakāya*.
If the essence of the Dharma were established, the marks and signs would likewise be established;
however, because Bodhisattvas possess a mind of grasping when they emerge from meditative absorption,
they grasp the marks and signs perceived according to their respective stages and positions as being fixed and real.
Having already demonstrated that the essence is true, one instead gives rise to doubt:
"Since it has been said that Buddhas are named for their unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta*),
how is it that all Buddhas achieve the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*)?"
Since the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) have already been accomplished, they must not be unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
If the Buddha were unconditioned, the marks and signs would not be the Buddha.
How, then, could one seek the marks and signs while contemplating the Dharma-body (dharmakāya)?
Because they do not contemplate reality,
although they practice, they do not achieve fulfillment;
this is due to their harboring doubt.
In the future, one will no longer cultivate the marks and signs;
now, however, I wish to manifest that mind of doubt and attachment so that it may contemplate the Dharma-body.
One attains the true essence by perfecting the marks and signs;
since the marks and signs are themselves [the essence],
it is shown that one does not see the Buddha by means of the marks and signs.
Asaṅga, focusing on the reality of the essence, explains that one cultivates and studies so as to be fully endowed with the marks and signs;
Vasubandhu, addressing the removal of doubts and seeking higher realization, explains that the marks and signs manifest [as such] because they are not the Buddha himself.
Vasubandhu maintains this because both are of the same nature of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Taken together, these statements clarify the doubt.
Asaṅga, because the physical marks and signs differ,
opened them into two distinct types of endowment.
This section on the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) is divided into four parts:
question, answer, inquiry, and explanation.
First, the meaning of the question is as follows:
If one wishes to be fully endowed with the secondary marks (anuvyañjana), one should contemplate the Dharma-body.
The Dharma-body is fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks that follow and conform to the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya).
Are these secondary marks seen in the form-body (rūpakāya)?
The response to this inquiry can be seen [in the source text];
there is no need to cite it again.
The meaning of the commentary is as follows:
That which the Tathāgata has described as being complete with the marks and secondary characteristics of an emanation body— the Buddha-body—
is merely that which is perceived by the distracted mind according to its particular stage; it is not the Dharma-body.

If one can contemplate the Buddha’s Dharma-body by way of detachment from signs, then the physical body— endowed with the minor marks arising from the nature-virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—
and the perfectly accomplished true minor marks will be realized.
This is what is called being endowed with a physical body (*rūpakāya*).
Although both the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*) constitute the physical body,
it is by means of the secondary signs that the physical body is fully realized.

The collective designation for these distinct virtues is "form" (*rūpa*), just as the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is so called; it is termed "form" because it is not something to be grasped or clung to.
This is because, like those four aggregates, it does not function as a representation.
This general designation should likewise apply here.
Sūtra: "Subhūti, [from] the possession of all marks... Commentary: [It says: "To the possession of all marks... *Zàn* (Commentary) states: [The following].
Next, the fourth mark, the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), is revealed;
therefore, it is not characterized by grasping.
However, because the characteristics of the name-and-form-body (*nāmarūpakāya*) involve grasping, [it is so designated].

The distinct enumeration of the meaning of their arising serves to clarify those doubts through a series of questions and answers; this follows the same principle as the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*),
differing only in that while the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary marks are distinct, the textual treatment of them is separate.

Since these marks and secondary characteristics arise based upon the Truth (tathatā), although they do not depart from it, they are not identical to its essential nature; thus, when observed as distinct phenomena, they cannot be said to be non-existent.
Yet, when observed as being identical to that very nature, they cannot be said to be existent.
Since the Dharma-body, being devoid [of form],
lacks the primary and secondary marks, these marks are not non-Buddha; yet,
in relation to the Dharma-body, they are neither non-existent nor existent.
Therefore, one should not dogmatically insist upon seeking [the Buddha] in this way.
Based on this meaning, the treatise states a verse:
The Dharma-body is the ultimate essence; It is not that body of marks and signs.
Because the marks and signs are accomplished, yet it is not the case that this is not the Dharma-body,
it does not depart from the Dharma-body; since those two are not non-Buddha,
"accomplishment" is stated again, and there is neither duality nor existence.
Sūtra:
"Subhūti, do not entertain such a thought. Commentary:
Next, the fifth section below clarifies the perfection of speech.
This clarifies the eighteenth [point]: the doubt regarding what the Buddha has taught, which causes one to cultivate the perfect verbal karma of the Buddha-body.
Previously, it was explained that one seeks the karma of the Buddha-body through the primary marks and secondary signs.
The body is not in vain;
one preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Having abandoned attachment, one becomes fully endowed with the means to seek the body.
Furthermore, having already explained the methods of teaching and preaching— whether square or round—
if one clings to the existence of speech and seeks its completeness, then because there is something spoken,
there will necessarily be something left unsaid. How, then, could one fulfill the Buddha’s verbal karma?
Because the Buddha neither speaks nor does not speak,
he speaks. Within a single utterance,
he expounds the ocean of infinite sūtras and all the linguistic dharmas of all sentient beings.
A single word of exposition exhausts all things without remainder;
every speech and sound of all sentient beings is none other than the teaching of the Tathāgata.
One who can thus encompass them with the wheel [of Dharma] is such a person.
They are fully endowed with names and words,
for they speak through the realization that there is no speaking;
thus it is with all bodhisattvas.
Within the state of distraction, one is unable to accord with reality and yet speaks where there is nothing to speak;
consequently, one instead suspects that the Tathāgata has a real teaching of the Dharma,
for this does not accord with reality.
Although they study, they do not achieve full mastery;
because they harbor doubts,
they do not contemplate the principle of non-explanation.
Now, wishing to reveal that mind of doubt and attachment so that they may know there is nothing to be taught yet seek full realization,
he says: "The one who teaches the Dharma."
Regarding the phrase "no dharma can be taught" and so forth:
Asaṅga, by means of non-attachment, leads [the practitioner] to accord with the non-teaching while seeking the perfection of the Buddha’s verbal expression;
Vasubandhu, however, focuses on the manifestation of the meaning to harmonize with the principle, thereby resolving doubts concerning the Buddha having something to teach.
The five middle and lower phrases serve to refute objections and establish the proof;
these are the first two.
For example, one might ask whether the Buddha is real or conventional.
That is to say, regarding the explanation that there is something apart from suchness, it is immediately refuted by saying: "Do not form the notion that the Tathāgata has five things taught.
(Sūtra)
Why is this so? The commentary states:
This is an inquiry.
The Sūtra says:
"If one says [the Tathāgata exists] because he has reached what I have taught," the commentary states:
"This is an explanation.
If it is said that the Tathāgata [exists] with respect to both the ultimate and the conventional..."
It is just as if one were to speak while departing from suchness;
if one speaks of the substantial entities of the signifier and the signified as being "beyond words," then because there is something spoken, there is also something not spoken.
This is because one would fail to understand the meaning of the Tathāgata’s words as they are not fully articulated;
would this not be slandering the Buddha?
Thus says the Sūtra.
"Subhūti, this is what is called preaching the Dharma. The commentary states:
This establishes [the point] because the Dharma that is preached does not exceed words and meanings;
apart from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), there is nothing to be sought of itself.
As previously sought for the Buddha, he thus preaches the Dharma through both the characterized and the uncharacterized; he is able to preach while being without preaching.
Because there is nothing preached, there is nothing not preached.
One is able to fully explain all phenomena with a single word;
beyond what is spoken, there is nothing further to be said,
because speech is perfected.
This is called "teaching the Dharma.
The verse of the treatise says:
"As with the Buddha, so it is with the Dharma; there are two distinctions in what is taught."
Not departing from the dharma-realm, he teaches the Dharma without self-characteristics.
Next, the sixth section clarifies the perfection of the mind.
Within this, according to the treatise, there are six kinds of mind.
First, a single point of focus;
second, the mind of perfect awakening;
third, the establishment of the Dharma of great benefit.
Fourth, the dharma-body that gathers [beings];
fifth, the great mind that does not dwell in saṃsāra;
sixth, the pure mind in conduct and abiding.
Among these, the first station of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is revealed in the sūtra as the eighteenth.
Who could believe this, and who could doubt it?
However, this scripture also lacks this passage;
since it exists in other editions, it is listed here according to the Wei edition as follows:
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being preached, will give rise to faith?
The Buddha said:
Subhūti, they are neither sentient beings nor non-sentient beings. Why is this?
Regarding "sentient beings," the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings;
it is merely designated as "sentient beings.
The intended meaning here is as follows:
Just as the Buddha, a bodhisattva constantly keeps sentient beings in mind;
whether they are virtuous or non-virtuous, faithful or faithless,
he should always benefit them.
Yet they do not abandon them. However,
these bodhisattvas cannot give rise to thoughts of joy and so forth in the same manner as the Buddha,
for they fear that sentient beings might harbor evil, lack faith, or present difficult obstacles, which would be a cause for lamentation.
He then gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Since these previous words state that both the speaker and the spoken are all non-existent,
what kind of person could believe in such a profound Dharma?"
Regarding those who lack faith,
how can one give rise to compassion through the continuous aspect of compassionate concern?
Because of doubt, they do not [accept] the Dharma.
Thereafter, wishing to reveal that mind of doubt and attachment and to give rise to the station of mindfulness characterized by great compassion born of non-understanding,
it is said that sentient beings— whether ultimate or conventional— are neither existent nor non-existent.
Whether one has faith or lacks faith, they are neither ordinary nor noble;
therein, one must not dogmatically cling to the notions of right or wrong.
One should simply maintain mindfulness of equanimity, as in the case of the three types of mindfulness.
Furthermore, not abandoning sentient beings—compassion that arises from equanimity free from attachment—is called the "mindfulness station of the mind.
As for Vasubandhu’s [treatment], he focuses on those who possess faith; thus, he clarifies the question: "Who is capable of believing? while addressing those who harbor doubt.
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
The teaching and the teacher are profound; It is not that there are none capable of believing it;
It is not that there are no sentient beings, nor that they are sentient beings; They are neither noble ones, nor are they non-noble.
Sūtra:
Subhūti, is it ultimately that there is nothing to be attained? Commentary:
Next, the second section below clarifies the mind of perfect awakening.
This reveals the nineteenth [point]: the doubt regarding the attainment of the fruit of realization.
Prior to practicing the causal conduct for the supreme fruit of Bodhi, mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) were clarified as the primary factors.
The wisdom of great compassion necessarily arises from the fulfillment of the fruit; once the fruit is perfected, it flows forth to accord with and bring about perfect enlightenment.
To achieve perfect enlightenment, one must immediately practice the supreme, wondrous conduct of both the conditioned and the unconditioned;
yet, because bodhisattvas do not depart from the notions of self and dharmas,
they cannot possess these two types of conduct as fully as the Buddha does.
They further doubt that the Buddha’s practice is not the supreme practice,
raising this suspicion:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata remain apart from non-attainment and non-practice?"
"This supreme realization is attained through successive practice and leads to the realization of awakening;
yet now you cause me to practice two paths.
Because of this grasping, although I practice, I deviate from perfect enlightenment."
Because of doubt, they further lack the desire to practice;
now, in order to reveal that mind of doubting attachment, the True Principle is taught.
Although there is not a single dharma to be practiced, [it is taught].
If one departs from conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is no means by which to realize it through the practice of skillful means (*upāya*).
Asaṅga, with respect to the elimination of grasping, causes [beings] to train; this is called the "mind of perfect awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*).
Vasubandhu, with respect to manifesting doubt, causes [beings] to cultivate; this is called "manifesting the existence of doubt regarding the realization of the fruit."
The text below is divided into two parts:
first, Subhūti poses a question;
second, the Tathāgata provides the answer.
This is the first [point].
Throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one practices both truths (*satya*) simultaneously;
thus, the perfect enlightenment attained—whether as cause or as fruit—is realized.
Is it not because there is nothing to be attained for them?
Sūtra: "In this way, in this way, Subhūti. Commentary: [End of commentary].
The response below has two parts:
first, it clarifies that the fruit of bodhi is non-apprehendable;
second, it clarifies that the causal path of awakening is non-apprehendable.
This further consists of two parts:
first, the fruit of the dharma-body;
second, the fruit of the reward-body.
The beginning, middle, and end each consist of three parts:
first, the introduction; next, the explanation; and finally, the conclusion.
This is the first [part].
In response to the preceding inquiry as to whether cause and effect are non-apprehendable,
it is now stated that such is the very nature of bodhi.
[Sūtra]:
"I do not perceive even the slightest dharma that can be attained in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

However, because the practice of the Bodhisattvas is as vast as space and the Dharma-realm, their practice only comes to an end when these reach their limit; therefore, it cannot be described.
It would be the same as the followers of the Two Vehicles who abandon the mind of great compassion to seek cessation and extinction.
He then stopped him, saying, "Do not entertain such thoughts.
[The Sūtra asks:
"For what reason? [The Commentary] says:
This is the inquiry.
The Sūtra says:
"From the arousal of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* up to the characteristic of cessation. The Commentary says:
This is the explanation:
one who has resolved to attain enlightenment (bodhicitta) is able to abide in True Suchness (tathatā).
While True Suchness is within the bonds of affliction, it is not oppressed by suffering.
Although they abide in nirvana, it is not the same as the severance of delusions;
thus, those who have resolved their minds attain superior patience and wisdom,
in accordance with the dharmas in which they dwell.
Yet they are able to penetrate [reality] without wearying of saṃsāra,
nor do they delight in nirvāṇa;
it is said that from their first aspiration, throughout many kalpas of saṃsāra, they extensively practice sublime conduct.
If one reaches the fruit of Buddhahood and manifests birth and death to benefit sentient beings,
such benefit necessarily relies upon superior merit.
Although merit is not the direct cause for the fruit of Buddhahood, it is indispensable for its realization.
Because it provides auxiliary support for the wisdom that realizes [the truth],
one attains the dharmakāya without losing meritorious activity;
for this reason, it is also said to have the characteristic of cessation.
Regarding this meaning, the treatise composes a verse:
Because it does not lose the cause of merit, And because of that superior retribution,
One attains supreme patience and does not lose it, For one has attained the stainless fruit.
[Sūtra]:
Subhūti, [even if one] were to practice the giving of the seven treasures... [Commentary]:
The following clarifies non-abiding in the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
The text is divided into two parts.
The first clarifies that although one possesses merit, one is not afflicted by suffering;
the second clarifies that while one undergoes retribution, one does not dwell in attachment.
This section consists of two parts:
first, the presentation of the inferior, and second, the revelation of the superior.
This is the former.
Fearing that the bodhisattvas might give rise to such thoughts—
that if they do not abide in nirvāṇa, they would be oppressed by the sufferings of saṃsāra—
he [spoke] in order to eliminate their minds of attachment and doubt.
This is because it is taught that there is merit and no suffering.
To cite an example: when an ordinary person gives jewels as a cause for merit, they may receive the retribution of a Wheel-Turning King, Śakra, or Brahmā;
yet even these are not perfectly supreme and are still subject to the pressure of suffering.
How much more so, then, is this true for the superior merit of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
As it is said in the sutras:
"Even a Wheel-Turning Sage King, by virtue of his meager merit, shall attain freedom from illness and other such benefits."
[Sūtra]:
"Furthermore, if there is another person who attains such merit... [Commentary]:
This reveals its superiority.
Just as with the merit of an ordinary person’s gift of jewels described previously,
although such a person remains within the cycle of birth and death, they shall not be oppressed by suffering;
how much more so for one who, being a superior person like a Buddha, knows that all phenomena lack those two types of self and thereby accomplishes the three patiences?
Having attained mastery over conditioned phenomena,
they are not produced by the power of karma or afflictions;
all their merit surpasses that of the former.
And are they further oppressed by suffering?
Regarding the two kinds of selflessness:
first, the selflessness of persons; second, the selflessness of phenomena.
Regarding the "three types of patience":
because one understands the principle of the two kinds of selflessness,
one is able [to apply it] to the three natures.
In this order, there arise the patience regarding the non-arising of the nature of suffering,
the patience regarding natural non-arising,
and the patience regarding the non-arising of afflictions and suffering.
Sūtra:
Subhūti, because he does not accept any merit whatsoever... Commentary:
The following clarifies that while one receives retribution, one does not dwell in or become attached to it.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the heading; second, the question; and third, the explanation.
This is the first.
This explains the reason why the aforementioned merit is superior:
because by realizing there is no self, one achieves patience (*kṣānti*),
and thus does not grasp at the merit performed.
[Sūtra]:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha... up to "...does not accept merit. [Commentary]:
This section contains the question.
Previously, the Buddha spoke of seeking the provisions for merit;
immediately prior to that, he further stated that merit is supreme.
In the former instance, this refers to the merit that a bodhisattva should receive.
"What, then, does it mean that one does not accept merit?
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva... up to... does not accept merit. The Commentary says:
This is the explanation.
There are two kinds of feeling (*vedanā*):
first, that which is experienced through non-attachment (*alobha*).
Second is attachment through grasping and receiving.
If this were non-attachment and untainted merit,
one should then receive it and not abide in nirvāṇa.
If one were attached to tainted merit,
then one would not undergo or abide within birth and death; therefore, because it causes one to experience [the cycle],
it is said that the bodhisattva’s seeking of the provisions of merit is superior to the former.
This is now taught so that one should not be greedily attached to what is performed;
thus it is said that a bodhisattva does not "accept" merit.
This is not intended to cause the total abandonment of merit.
The verse of the treatise says:
Because the marks of physical excellence arise from merit, I shall again employ analogies.
This merit has no [karmic] retribution; Thus one experiences it without grasping.
Sūtra:
Subhūti, [this is] the meaning spoken by me. Commentary:
Next follows the sixth [section], dwelling with a pure mind.

For the sake of transforming sentient beings, he gathers and performs the superior conditioned activities of the conduct, abiding, supernormal powers, skillful means, preaching the Dharma, and the cycle of existence;
this superior practice of wisdom is called the "abiding in conduct."
This is what is called "abiding.

now, in order to elucidate it, the following passage begins.
This section consists of three parts.
First, purity of conduct in the postures of walking and staying;
second, purity of conduct in the mastery over the body of name-and-form;
third, purity of conduct in non-attachment.
Due to conditions and responsive resonance, it appears as if there is someone coming;
by observing speech without attachment, one accomplishes great supernormal powers and remains free from defiled clinging toward the preaching of the Dharma and other such activities.
Now, the complete explanation is given so that he may seek what is to be learned through such a sequence:

Causing them to cultivate the purity of the Buddha-fruit through various modes of conduct;
the Bodhisattva thus seeks the stage of Buddhahood above.

it is said that the Tathāgata truly possesses knowledge of the future and thus gives rise to training and study.
This is because, by not speaking [of this], one remains deluded regarding the truth.

One might raise this doubt, saying:
"Since it was previously stated that such merit has no retribution and no outflowing retribution (*anāsrava-vipāka*)," [how can it have knowledge?].
How can one manifest appearance and disappearance, coming and going, and teach the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
so that beings may behold this and derive benefit?
To have coming and going is itself the fruit of outflows (*āsrava*).
Furthermore, how can one be free from suffering and affliction?
Because of clinging, one fails to achieve success despite seeking it;
because of doubt, one does not cultivate the causes for achievement.
Now, wishing to sever that mind of doubt and attachment,
and to cause them to rejoice in the superior application of the response,
it is taught that there is truly no characteristic of coming or going.
Asaṅga, focusing on the removal of attachment while seeking higher goals, names this "purity of conduct in postures and movements" (īryāpathaviśuddhi).
Vasubandhu, focusing on the severing of doubt, identifies it as "severing the doubt regarding transformation and non-utility."
The passage following the text has three parts:
first, restating the tenet to demonstrate its incorrectness;
second, interrogating the basis for that incorrectness.
Next follows the explanation of the reasons for this;
this is the first [point].
First comes cultivation, followed by non-cultivation.

Sūtra:

The true Tathāgata is serene and eternally abiding;
his response-body and transformation-bodies are neither identical to nor different from the true Dharma-realm.

If one speaks according to the various responses to conditions, it may appear as though there is coming and going through multiple gates; yet, if one speaks from the perspective of the nature of merit that encompasses all characteristics, there is no coming or going.

Since phenomena are merely manifestations of the mind,
how could these pure modes of conduct possess the characteristics of coming and going? Therefore,
