The verse of the treatise says:
The emanation bodies of the past and future Buddhas, The Tathāgata is eternally unmoving within that realm of phenomena; Neither identical nor different [from it].
[Sūtra]:
Subhūti, would this amount to much? [Commentary]:
Next follows the second [section], which refutes the purity of the body’s mastery over names and forms (nāmarūpa) regarding movement and abiding.
This eliminates the twenty-seventh doubt concerning whether the true and the manifested are identical or different.
It was previously clarified that, relying on the truth, one responds according to conditions;
though free from the characteristics of coming and going, one manifests dignified conduct.
Yet, the extensive manifestation of supernatural powers and transformative functions,
skillful means and mastery,
and the various superior practices of wisdom would not exist without this.
Furthermore, they are unable to give rise to pure modes of conduct;
yet these bodhisattvas, not having abandoned their grasping mind,
are unable to train in the Buddha’s arousal of wise activity.
Returning to the doubt regarding whether the supernatural powers possessed by the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) are identical to or distinct from the true dharmadhātu:
if they were distinct, [then...]
Since the Truth is inherently motionless,
any wisdom that arises apart from the Truth must be delusory.
Just as external gifts should not be undertaken,
if [the mind] were one,
it would be suchness itself.
There should not be any movement or activity that exists separately from reality.
How, then, could I be forced to give rise to it?
Because of this clinging, although one practices, one is unable to give rise to it.
Because of doubt, one does not cultivate the causes for its arousal.
Now, wishing to sever that mind of doubtful clinging,
I cause them to rely upon the truth and give rise to signless wisdom (*animitta-prajñā*).

The teaching of the world as being like fine dust illustrates that the realm and the dust are neither identical nor different; this reveals that the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the true body (*dharmakāya*) are likewise neither identical nor different.
Asaṅga, focusing on the removal of attachments, explains that the ability to give rise to [manifestations] is termed "mastery over the arising and dwelling of the pure body of name-and-form."
Regarding Vasubandhu’s treatment of the severance of doubt, he cultivates a single cause called "severing the doubt concerning the identity or difference between the true and the emanated.
The text is divided into six parts;
the first is the skillful means of non-perception.
Second, that which is not conceptualized as it is;
third, that which the mind does not conceptualize;
fourth, the phenomena with respect to which one does not conceptualize.
Fifth, by what means is there non-discrimination?
Sixth, how is there non-discrimination?
Regarding the first [of these], there are two [sections].
Initially, the Tathāgata used the analogy of motes of dust to instruct [Subhūti] to analyze and contemplate the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Subsequently, Subhūti used the analogy of the world-system to clarify that the characteristics of the aggregates are empty.
Regarding the initial section, there are further six parts.
First the question, second the answer, third the inquiry, fourth the explanation, fifth the objection, and sixth the resolution.
This is the first [section].
Now, the term "world" (*loka*) conveys two meanings: "commonality" and "metaphor."
The first metaphor illustrates the true nature (*tathatā*) as the totality of the *dharmakāya*.
The second metaphor illustrates the general characteristics of the appropriated aggregates (*skandha*).
Furthermore, the multitude of atoms (*paramāṇu*) also serves as a metaphor for two meanings.
The first simile illustrates the manifestation of countless transformation bodies;
the second simile illustrates the analysis of the composite nature of the aggregates,
because one clings to the characteristics of the aggregates without analyzing them.
Being unable to accord with reality, one gives rise to the causes of transformation;
using the world as a metaphor for the characteristics of the aggregates,
one causes them to contemplate [the aggregates] as being shattered into atoms.
Because the afflictions of clinging to phenomena have been completely severed,
one is able to realize the Truth and,
based upon that Truth, manifest transformations.
The Real and its transformations are neither identical nor different.
It is like when the world is shattered and many particles arise;
the totality of the world and its constituent particles are neither identical nor different.
In order to clarify these two points,
he asked: "Subhūti, if the three-thousandfold world system were broken down into atoms,
would the multitude of those atoms be numerous?"
The Treatise says:
"The world is reduced to fine dust"—this metaphor demonstrates that meaning;
"the fine dust is ground into powder" demonstrates the manifestation of the exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa*).
[Sutra]:
"Very much so, World-Honored One. [Commentary]:
This is the answer.

Since there are already many particles, how could there be a real constituent element (*dhātu*)? How much less could there be a real body? By observing the external, one realizes that internally there is no characteristic of a body;
thus, attachment and delusion are completely exhausted.
Having realized the true Dharma-body,
one is able to manifest transformations based upon that true body; thus,
the transformations are distinct from the true marks.
The Real and the Transformation are not one;
the Transformation does not depart from the Real.
The Real and the Transformation are not different.
Just as external objects are not one,
yet because they lack a separate essence they are not different;
it is to clarify this analogical meaning that [the text] says "very many."
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
It is not a collection, yet it is a collection; It is not merely one, nor is it the locus of a collection; It is not a differentiated metaphor.
"Non-aggregated" indicates that the entities of the collected objects are distinct from one another;
"therefore aggregated" indicates that many distinct objects are gathered together to form a collective sphere (*dhātu*).
Since the general and the particular are distinct, they are not one.
The phrase "the place of aggregation" indicates the location of subtle aggregations.
This refers to the aggregate realm (*dhātu*).
As for the statement "not that," it means that there is no realm-object (*viṣaya*) apart from the aggregate realm.
The general and the particular are without difference; this is not a dissimilar example.
The Sūtra asks:
"For what reason? The Commentary says:
This is an inquiry.
If this [object] were substantially real, one would grasp and seek it as a sensory object;
if it were not substantially real, one should not speak of it as being "many."
As for why it is said that they are "very many," the Sūtra states:
"If these atoms were further analyzed down to the multitude of atoms... The Commentary says:
This is the explanation.
It clarifies that when the Buddha spoke of "dust" (objects), he did not mean they exist as substantial realities.
If they were substantial realities, [the following would apply].
Although the Buddha did not speak of it, worldly people know it for themselves;
why would the Buddha discuss it in the sutras?
Why is this so? The commentary states:
This is an objection.
If sensory objects have no reality, for what reason does the Buddha speak of them?
What is the reason for this statement?
The Sūtra says:
"The Buddha spoke of atoms as being a 'multitude of atoms'. The Commentary states:
This is the supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
The Buddha taught that by using the metaphor of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), one deconstructs the characteristics of the body,
because one does not perceive any characteristic of the union between form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
It is able to distance itself from the grasping of delusions;
relying on the Truth, it gives rise to transformations.
Like the arising of dust from a realm, these are neither identical nor different.
To clarify this meaning:
what is conventionally designated as a "minute particle" (paramāṇu) is not substantially existent.
The multitude of internal and external objects are merely provisional retributions.
Below, by breaking down and negating the aggregates (*skandha*), form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and mental factors (*caitta-saṃskāra*), one provisionally designates "subtle atoms" (*paramāṇu*);
this serves as a metaphor for the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Arising based on reality, it is neither identical nor different;
yet it is spoken of as a multitude of subtle atoms.
Thus says the Sūtra.
"Bhagavān, Tathāgata, you have arrived at this world. The commentary states:
From here below, Subhūti uses the metaphor of a world to reveal that the aggregate as a whole is empty.
This section is divided into three parts.
This consists of three parts: first, the initial statement; second, the inquiry; and third, the explanation.
This is the first part.
Regarding that which the Tathāgata has spoken of as the "trichiliocosm":
The aggregate world is formed by the accumulation of subtle particles;
it serves as a metaphor for the internal body and the world of sentient beings.
That which is comprised of the five aggregates for the most part is not the world itself,
because that which is so composed lacks any substantial reality.
Internally, too, there is no intrinsic nature.
That which is called a "world" is merely a conventional designation for a world.

By means of conventional designations, one contemplates the internal body through the analogy of external objects as lacking any real characteristic; thus, one is able to abandon attachment and delusion.
Furthermore, just as external objects are composed of a collection of atoms and possess no substantial essence or form, so it is with the internal body.
It is called a "world" (*loka*) simply because it arises from a multitude of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The Dharmakāya that is manifested is formed by encompassing all virtues and is devoid of any marks;
it is only because it can arise [in manifestation] that it is termed the Nirmāṇakāya.
[Sūtra]:
Why is this so? [Commentary]:
This is the introduction of the inquiry.
Why is it that the external world, the internal body, and the dharma-body are all without marks?
The Sūtra says:
"If a world is reached, it is but a single unified mark (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*). Commentary: [As follows].
The following explains the reasons for this.
It consists of two parts:
first, the direct refutation; second, the manifestation of emptiness.
This is the first [point].
If one says that external objects and the internal body are real, this is a "composite mark" (*saṃghāta-lakṣaṇa*).
A "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to grasping (*abhiniveśa*).
This refers to the grasping that both internal and external phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics,
yet conceiving of a collection of provisional aggregations as a single entity;
since there is already such a grasping mind at work, [it is called "clinging"].
Consequently, afflictions arise.
How, then, can the signless Dharma-body be manifested?
Sūtra:
"The Tathāgata has preached that 'one-union' is called the 'characteristic of one-union. Commentary:
The following passage clarifies emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The text is further divided into two parts.
At first there was Subhūti;
afterwards the Tathāgata was accomplished.
This is the beginning.
The Tathāgata has constantly taught that the so-called "unified whole" of the external world and the internal body is entirely empty in its essence,
because while it appears as an object of cognition, it lacks reality in the ultimate sense.
Yet within ultimate truth, even mental states do not exist.
It is merely in accordance with those mental states that they are designated as a "unified whole.
Thus says the Sūtra:
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, up to this point it is ineffable. The commentary says:
Below, the Buddha reiterates and establishes [the meaning].
Within this, there are two parts.
In the beginning, the essence was truly non-existent, yet later it was falsely grasped as existent;
this is the first point.
That is to say, the Buddha thoroughly understood that external objects and the internal body lack any real intrinsic nature.
Regarding that which can be spoken:
the Sūtra says, "But ordinary persons are greedily attached to those things. The commentary states:
This is the false attachment to existence.
Because ordinary beings do not understand that the essence is empty and non-existent,
they merely follow sounds and give rise to false attachment to phenomena.
Because the grasping at phenomena arises, the grasping at a self also arises,
thereby increasing craving, attachment, and all other afflictions. Thus,
a verse in the treatise says:
Merely following the sounds, ordinary people grasp at the sūtras erroneously.
Subhūti has reached the meaning of what was taught. [The commentary] says:
The following clarifies that as long as there is no conceptual differentiation, there can be no seeing.
Previously, the objects of perception—the self and phenomena—were refuted;
now, the perceiving mind that views the self and phenomena is refuted.
The mind that perceives is precisely the conceptualization that has arisen;
now, by reversing this, one causes it to become a non-conceptualizing mind,
and thus it is said to be "like that which is not conceptually discriminated."
The text is divided into four parts:
question, answer, inquiry, and explanation.
This is the first.
The Buddha taught that there are two emptinesses regarding the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
The first is for the purpose of establishing the principle of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*),
which means revealing that there is no such thing as the characteristic of a self as it is grasped [by ignorance].
It is solely because of the mind that perceives a false self.
Second, in order to establish the principle of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*),
it is taught that the essence of this perception of a self is likewise not a real phenomenon.
Since there is no seeing because it does not exist,
when one observes in this way, in reality there are no two types of seeing.
As for the mind that grasps:
This is precisely the skillful means for entering the corresponding samāpatti;
it does not mean that knowing the non-existence of the grasped self and dharmas, and taking the perceiving mind as the entry point, constitutes the skillful means.
The verse of the treatise says:
"The path is not attained through non-duality.
This is because the Buddha wished to destroy their views of selfhood and their doubts regarding the [existence of] self and dharmas.
Question: Subhūti, does anyone speak of a real self to the Buddha, such that the view of a self would be eternally empty?
[The Sūtra says:
"World-Honored One, it is as you have explained. Commentary: This praises the meaning of what has been taught.
This is the answer.
The "view of self" is provisionally posited in order to refute the two types of grasping;
it does not mean that it truly exists.
Regarding this essence of the view of self:
if one says that the Buddha taught a real self,
then that person does not understand the Buddha’s emptiness.
[Sūtra]:
Why is this? [Commentary]:
This is an inquiry.
Since there is no real seeing of the Buddha, for what reason is it said?
And as for saying "I see," for what reason is that?
[The Sūtra says:]
"The World-Honored One arrives at the sight of the person. The commentary states:
This is the explanation.
There are three parts within the text.
This refers to restating what is not a [true] bond.
When the Blessed One spoke of the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and so forth,
it was for the purpose of eliminating the obstacle of clinging to a self and to phenomena (*ātmadharmagrāha*).
This is spoken as a provisional designation to cause the cessation of false conceptualization;
it is not truly existent.
Since these views of self and so forth lack a self that exists as an object, how could there be a subject that perceives?
Arising from beginningless habitual tendencies and false discrimination,
it is called a subtle hindrance because it fundamentally obstructs the vision of ultimate truth;
it prevents one from seeing the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) and the two kinds of selflessness.
Because they are [in fact] free from them,
they are conventionally designated as "view of self" and so forth.
To clarify this meaning, the treatise states a verse:
Seeing me yet not seeing [me], this unreal and false perception is a subtle obstruction;
it is explained in the *Tathatā-viparyāsa-parihāra-sūtra*.
Regarding "those who have set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," the commentary says:
This reveals which persons do not engage in conceptual discrimination.
As for those being excluded here:
Ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of the two vehicles—both those in training and those beyond training—are subject to two views according to their respective capacities;
they regard these as truly existent and have not yet realized the principle of the two kinds of emptiness.
Only Bodhisattvas possess the superior wisdom that enables them to aspire toward enlightenment;
because they have severed the two obscurations,
they may be called those who are non-conceptualizing.
Sūtra: Regarding all phenomena. Commentary:
This clarifies which phenomena are not to be conceptually differentiated.
Those of the two vehicles who do not seek the universal are not without discrimination regarding all things;
the bodhisattva differs from them.
Regarding all phenomena, one contemplates the dharma of selflessness and does not engage in conceptual discrimination.
The Sūtra says:
"One should thus arrive at faith and understanding. The Commentary states:
What does this reveal regarding the means of non-conceptualization?
It indicates that within whatever meditative concentration or wisdom there may be, one must necessarily rely on these conditions for it to be non-conceptual.
Furthermore, these means are categorized into three types: general and specific.
If it is based on the aspect of the meaning of the tranquility of all objects, it is called *śamatha*;
this belongs to the category of cessation (*śamatha*).
If it is based on the aspect of the meaning of the discernment of all objects, it is called *vipaśyanā*.
This is the stage of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
When these two stages are in equilibrium, it is called *samādhi*;
this is "equipoise" (*samāhita*).
Although their substance is not distinct, their meanings differ.
That which relies upon [the basis] to produce wisdom is precisely the fundamental ultimate wisdom;
it is termed "knowledge."
Wisdom arises based on contemplation;
because this is precisely the subsequently attained conventional wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
it is termed "vision" (*darśana*).
If the wisdom arising from meditative concentration (samādhi) illuminates both the ultimate and conventional truths in unification,
it is called "resolute belief" (adhimukti).
Through this, one understands that the three— knowledge, vision, and resolute belief— are characterized by their respective general and specific states of quiescence and illumination.
Non-conceptual wisdom is able to abandon the mind that discriminates between self and phenomena;
it is precisely the skillful means of non-conceptuality.
To elucidate this meaning, the treatise composes a verse as follows:
Through the two wisdoms and samādhi, one thus attains the sūtra of detachment.
One does not give rise to the conceptualization of dharmas. Commentary:
This clarifies what non-conceptualization is and what its mode of activity is.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation.
This is the first [point].
"Dharma" refers to the object;
"characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the mind.
Relying on the wisdom of true samādhi, one is free from the characteristics of subject and object;
this is precisely the aspect of non-conceptual practice.
Sūtra:
